courses.title: Ch 8 · Strings
courses.summary: Creating strings, positive and negative indexing, immutability, concatenation, repetition, membership, comparison, slicing, traversal, built-in methods and classic programs like palindrome and vowel counting.
outcomes: Learners can index and slice strings correctly
Learners can traverse strings with loops
Learners can use common string methods
Learners can write string-processing programs

scenes.text: Riya stores her name as name = "VIDYA".
Each letter sits in a numbered box starting at 0.
She cannot change a single letter in place — strings are immutable.

steps.title: Creating strings
steps.body: A **string** is a sequence of characters enclosed in single ('…'), double ("…") or triple quotes ('''…''' or """…""" for multi-line). Empty string: "".

steps.title: Indexing
steps.body:
Positive index from 0 (left); negative index from −1 (right).

For s = "VIDYA": s[0] = 'V', s[4] = 'A', s[−1] = 'A', s[−5] = 'V'. s[5] → **IndexError**. len(s) = 5.

steps.title: Immutability
steps.body: Strings cannot be changed in place: s[0] = "B" → **TypeError**. Create a new string instead: s = "B" + s[1:].

steps.title: Solved example 2: Fixing a typo
steps.body: s = "Pyhton" → s = s[:2] + "th" + s[4:] → "Python".

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting indexes at 1.
- Trying to assign to s[i].
- Using s[len(s)] (out of range).

activity.prompt: Read a word and print its first character, its last character and its length on three lines.
activity.solution:
s = input()
print(s[0])
print(s[-1])
print(len(s))
activity.hint: Use s[0], s[-1] and len(s).

quiz.why: String indexing starts at 0. In 'HELLO', index 0 is H and index 1 is E.
A negative index counts from the end, so s[−1] is the last character.
Strings are immutable, so their characters cannot be changed in place.
len() counts the characters in a string. 'India' has 5 letters, so len('India') = 5.
'abc' has indexes 0, 1, 2 only. Index 3 is out of range, so s[3] raises IndexError.

scenes.text: Riya wants only the year from "26-11-2026".
She also wants to join first and last names.
Slicing, concatenation and repetition do the job.

steps.title: Operations
steps.body:
- **Concatenation** +: "Good" + "Day" → "GoodDay".
- **Repetition** *: "ha" * 3 → "hahaha".
- **Membership** in / not in: "ell" in "hello" → True.
- **Comparison**: compares character codes left to right ("apple" < "banana" → True; "Z" < "a" → True).

steps.title: Slicing
steps.body:
s[start:stop:step] — from start up to *but not including* stop.

For s = "26-11-2026": s[0:2] = "26"; s[6:] = "2026"; s[:5] = "26-11"; s[::2] = "2-122" (characters at indices 0, 2, 4, 6, 8); s[::-1] = "6202-11-62" (reversed). Slicing never raises IndexError — out-of-range bounds are trimmed.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: s = "COMPUTER": s[1:4] = "OMP"; s[−3:] = "TER"; s[:3] + s[−3:] = "COMTER"; s[::−1] = "RETUPMOC".

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: name = "Riya"; surname = "Sharma"; full = name + " " + surname → "Riya Sharma". "-" * 10 → "----------".

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including the stop index.
- Thinking s[10:20] on a short string raises an error (it returns "").
- Adding a string and a number with +.

activity.prompt: Read a date in the form DD-MM-YYYY and print the year, month and day on three lines using slicing.
activity.solution:
d = input()
print(d[6:])
print(d[3:5])
print(d[0:2])
activity.hint: Day is d[0:2], month d[3:5], year d[6:].

quiz.why: The * operator repeats a string, so 'ab' * 3 = 'ababab'.
A slice s[1:4] starts at index 1 and stops before index 4. In 'PYTHON' that is indexes 1, 2, 3, which is 'YTH'.
A slice with step −1, s[::−1], goes through the string backwards. So it reverses s.
The 'in' operator checks for a substring. 'cat' appears inside 'concatenate', so the result is True.
Slicing beyond the end is safe in Python. It does not raise an error and just gives an empty string.

scenes.text: Riya wants to count vowels in a sentence.
She loops over each character and checks it.
Traversal is the key to most string programs.

steps.title: Two ways to traverse
steps.body:
1. for ch in s: … (each character).
2. for i in range(len(s)): … s[i] … (with index).
3. while i < len(s): … i += 1.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Count vowels
steps.body: s = "Education"; count = 0; for ch in s.lower(): if ch in "aeiou": count += 1 → **5** (e, u, a, i, o).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Print with index
steps.body: for i in range(len("abc")): print(i, "abc"[i]) → 0 a / 1 b / 2 c.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting case: "A" is not in "aeiou" unless you lower() first.
- Modifying the string inside the loop (strings are immutable; build a new one).

activity.prompt: Read a line of text and print the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u, either case).
activity.hint: Convert to lowercase, then check membership in "aeiou".

quiz.why: A for loop over a string runs once per character. 'hi' has 2 characters, so the loop runs 2 times.
The vowels in 'APPLE' are A and E, so there are 2.
range(len(s)) gives 0 to len(s) − 1, which are all valid indexes of s.

quiz.q: To build a reversed string in a loop, start with…
quiz.why: To build a string by adding characters, start with an empty string rev = ''. A list, 0 or None would not join with characters in the same way.
String comparison is case-sensitive. The lowercase 'a' is not in 'AEIOU', so the result is False.

scenes.text: Usernames come with extra spaces and mixed case: "  RiYa ".
strip() and lower() clean them.
find(), count(), split() and more do the rest.

steps.title: Case and checks
steps.body: len(s) · s.lower() · s.upper() · s.title() (first letter of each word capital) · s.capitalize() · s.swapcase() · s.islower() · s.isupper() · s.isalpha() · s.isdigit() · s.isalnum() · s.isspace() · s.startswith(x) · s.endswith(x).

steps.title: Search, clean, split
steps.body: s.count(sub) · s.find(sub) (index or −1) · s.index(sub) (error if not found) · s.replace(old, new) · s.strip() / lstrip() / rstrip() · s.split(sep) → list · sep.join(list) → string · s.partition(sep) → 3-tuple (before, sep, after).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: s = "  Hello World  " → s.strip() = "Hello World"; s.strip().lower() = "hello world"; "hello world".title() = "Hello World"; "Hello World".count("o") = 2; "Hello World".find("World") = 6; "Hello".find("z") = −1.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: "a,b,c".split(",") → ['a', 'b', 'c']; "-".join(['2026', '11', '26']) → "2026-11-26"; "user@mail.com".partition("@") → ('user', '@', 'mail.com'); "banana".replace("a", "o") → "bonono".

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting methods to change the original (they return new strings).
- Using index() when the substring may be absent (use find()).
- Calling join on the list instead of the separator: list.join(",") is wrong.

activity.prompt: Read a sentence and print the number of words in it (words are separated by spaces; ignore extra spaces), then print the sentence in title case.
activity.solution:
s = input()
print(len(s.split()))
print(s.title())
activity.hint: split() without arguments ignores extra spaces.

quiz.why: upper() changes all letters to uppercase, so 'hello'.upper() = 'HELLO'.
find() returns the index of the first match, or −1 if the text is not found. 'd' is not in 'abc', so it returns −1.
split('-') cuts the string at each hyphen and returns a list: ['a', 'b', 'c'].
isdigit() returns True if every character is a digit. '123' has only digits, so it is True.
strip() removes spaces from both ends of a string. ' x '.strip() gives 'x'.

lessons.title: String programs: palindrome, reverse and more

scenes.text: “madam” reads the same backwards.
Riya writes a program to test any word.
Common exam programs use these patterns.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Palindrome
Solved example 2: Count characters by type
steps.body: s = "Class 11-A!" → uppercase 2 (C, A), lowercase 4, digits 2, others 3 (space, -, !).

steps.title: Solved example 3: Reverse each word
steps.body: " ".join(w[::-1] for w in "I love Python".split()) → "I evol nohtyP".

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to normalise case before comparing.
- Counting a space as a letter.

activity.prompt: Read a word and print Palindrome if it reads the same backwards (ignore uppercase/lowercase differences), else print Not palindrome.
activity.hint: Compare s.lower() with its reverse s[::-1].

quiz.why: 'level' reads the same backwards, so it is a palindrome. Its reverse is still 'level'.
In 'MyPy' the capital letters are M and P, so there are 2.
join() puts the separator between the items. ' '.join(['a', 'b']) = 'a b'.
To compare strings without caring about case, convert both to lowercase (or uppercase) with lower().
isalnum() is True only if all characters are letters or digits. '!' is neither, so 'Hi!'.isalnum() is False.

questions.q: s = "PYTHON"; s[0] =
questions.why: Indexing starts from 0, so s[0] is the first character, 'P'.

questions.q: Strings are…
questions.why: Strings are immutable. Their characters cannot be changed after creation.
An empty string has no characters, so len('') = 0.
The + operator joins two strings (concatenation), so 'Hi' + '5' = 'Hi5'.

questions.q: s = "COMPUTER"; s[−3:] =
questions.why: s[−3:] starts three characters from the end and goes to the end. In 'COMPUTER' that is 'TER'.

questions.q: "banana".count("a") =
questions.why: 'banana' has the letter a in three places, so count('a') = 3.

questions.q: Assertion (A): s[0] = "X" raises an error. Reason (R): Strings are immutable.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Strings are immutable, so assigning to s[0] raises a TypeError.

questions.q: "hello world".title() =
questions.why: title() capitalises the first letter of each word, so 'hello world'.title() = 'Hello World'.

questions.q: s = "ABCDEFG"; s[1:6:2] =
questions.why: s[1:6:2] starts at index 1 and takes every second character up to index 5: indexes 1, 3, 5 which are B, D, F.

questions.q: "Python".find("th") =
questions.why: 'th' first appears at index 2 in 'Python' (P0, y1, t2, h3), so find returns 2.

questions.q: Output: print("ab" * 2 + "c")
questions.why: * is done before +. 'ab' * 2 = 'abab', and adding 'c' gives 'ababc'.

questions.q: "apple" < "Apple" is…
questions.why: Strings are compared by character codes. 'a' (97) is greater than 'A' (65), so 'apple' < 'Apple' is False.

questions.q: Output: s = "hello"; print(s.replace("l", "L", 1))
questions.why: replace('l', 'L', 1) changes only the first occurrence of 'l'. So 'hello' becomes 'heLlo'.

questions.q: Output: print("-".join("abc"))
questions.why: '-'.join('abc') puts '-' between the characters of the string, giving 'a-b-c'.

questions.q: Output: s = "Programming"; print(s[::-3])
questions.why: The string 'Programming' has 11 characters. With step −3 from the end, the indexes are 10, 7, 4, 1, giving g, m, r, r: 'gmrr'.

questions.q: Output: print("a,b,,c".split(","))
questions.why: Splitting on ',' keeps the empty string between the two commas. So the result is ['a', 'b', '', 'c'].

courses.title: Ch 9 · Lists
courses.summary: Creating and indexing lists, mutability, operations and slicing, traversal, list methods and built-in functions, nested lists, aliasing vs copying, lists in functions and classic list programs like linear search.
outcomes: Learners can create, index, slice and modify lists
Learners can use list methods correctly
Learners can explain aliasing and make copies
Learners can write list-processing programs

story.title: A shopping list you can edit

scenes.text: Riya’s list: ["milk", "bread", "eggs"].
She replaces bread with butter — lists can change.
Lists hold many values of any type, in order.

steps.title: Creating and indexing
steps.body:
A **list** is an ordered, **mutable** sequence of elements in square brackets: marks = [78, 85, 92]; mixed = [1, "two", 3.0, [4, 5]]; empty = [] or list().

Indexing like strings: marks[0] = 78; marks[−1] = 92. Nested: mixed[3][1] = 5.

steps.title: Mutability
steps.body: Elements can be changed in place: marks[1] = 88 → [78, 88, 92]. This is the key difference from strings and tuples.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Index out of range (L[4] for a 4-element list).
- Confusing [] (list) with () (tuple).

activity.prompt: Read 3 integers (separate lines) into a list, replace the middle element with 0, and print the list.
activity.solution:
L = []
for _ in range(3):
    L.append(int(input()))
L[1] = 0
print(L)
activity.hint: Index 1 is the middle of three elements.

quiz.why: Lists are mutable, so their items can be changed, added or removed after creation.
A negative index counts from the end, so L[−1] is the last element, 6.
list('hi') makes a list of the characters of the string: ['h', 'i'].
An empty list is written with square brackets, []. {} makes a dictionary and () a tuple.

scenes.text: Riya joins two class lists with +.
She takes only the top three scorers with slicing.
She loops through to find the total.

steps.title: Operations
steps.body:
- Concatenation: [1, 2] + [3] → [1, 2, 3].
- Repetition: [0] * 4 → [0, 0, 0, 0].
- Membership: 3 in [1, 2, 3] → True.
- Slicing: L[1:3], L[::−1] (reverse copy). Slices can also be assigned: L[0:2] = [9, 9].

steps.title: Traversal
steps.body: for x in L: … or for i in range(len(L)): … L[i] … (needed when you modify elements by index).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using for x in L: x = x * 2 expecting the list to change (it does not).
- [1, 2] + 3 → TypeError (use append or + [3]).

activity.prompt: Read n, then n integers (one per line). Print the sum and the average (as a float) on two lines.
activity.solution:
n = int(input())
L = []
for _ in range(n):
    L.append(int(input()))
total = 0
for x in L:
    total += x
print(total)
print(total / n)
activity.hint: Traverse the list to add up values; divide by n for the average.

quiz.why: Multiplying a list by 2 repeats its items, so [1, 2] * 2 = [1, 2, 1, 2].
L[1:3] takes indexes 1 and 2, so the result is [6, 7].
4 is not in [1, 2, 3], so the 'in' check gives False.
L[::−1] goes through the list backwards and makes a new reversed list. The original stays the same.

quiz.q: To modify elements by index, loop with…
quiz.why: To change items by index, loop over the indexes with range(len(L)). A plain 'for x in L' only gives the values.

scenes.text: Riya manages a class list: new students join, some leave.
She sorts names alphabetically.
List methods make it easy.

steps.title: Adding and removing
steps.body:
- append(x): add one element at end.
- extend(iterable): add many elements.
- insert(i, x): insert at index i.
- remove(x): remove first occurrence of x (ValueError if absent).
- pop(i): remove and return element at i (default last).
- del L[i] or del L[i:j]: delete by index/slice.
- clear(): empty the list.

steps.title: Searching, ordering, functions
steps.body:
- count(x), index(x).
- reverse(): reverses in place.
- sort(): sorts in place (sort(reverse=True) for descending); returns None.
- sorted(L): returns a new sorted list.
- len(), min(), max(), sum().

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: M = [5, 2, 8]; M.sort() → [2, 5, 8]; sorted(M, reverse=True) → [8, 5, 2] (M unchanged); max(M) = 8; sum(M) = 15; M.index(5) = 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- L = L.sort() → L becomes None.
- append([5, 9]) adds one nested list, not two elements.
- remove() takes a value, pop() takes an index.

activity.prompt: Read n, then n integers (one per line). Print the list sorted in ascending order, then the largest and smallest values on separate lines.
activity.starter:
n = int(input())
L = [int(input()) for _ in range(n)]
activity.solution:
n = int(input())
L = [int(input()) for _ in range(n)]
L.sort()
print(L)
print(max(L))
print(min(L))
activity.hint: Use L.sort(), then max() and min().

quiz.why: append adds its argument as one element, even if it is a list. So L has 3 elements: 1, 2 and [3, 4].
pop() with no argument removes and returns the last element of the list.
sort() sorts the list in place and returns None. It does not give back a sorted list.
The value 4 occurs twice in [4, 2, 4], so count(4) = 2.
remove(x) deletes the first occurrence of the value x. It does not work by index.

lessons.title: Nested lists, copying and lists in functions

scenes.text: Riya writes B = A and changes B — A changes too!
Both names point to the same list.
To get a real copy, she must copy it.

steps.title: Nested lists
steps.body: A list of lists acts like a table: M = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]; M[1][2] = 6; for row in M: for x in row: …

steps.title: Aliasing and copying
steps.body: B = A makes B an **alias** (same object; id(A) == id(B)). Changes through B appear in A. Real copies: B = A.copy(), B = list(A), B = A[:]. (For nested lists, these are shallow copies.)

steps.title: Lists as function arguments
steps.body: A list passed to a function is the same object; changes made inside the function (append, item assignment) are visible outside. Reassigning the parameter to a new list does not affect the caller.

steps.title: Solved example 2
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking B = A copies the list.
- Expecting a function to return a value when it only modifies the list.

activity.prompt: Define add_five(L) that adds 5 to every element of the list in place (no return). Read n and n integers, call the function and print the list.
activity.starter:
def add_five(L):
    pass

n = int(input())
L = [int(input()) for _ in range(n)]
activity.solution:
def add_five(L):
    for i in range(len(L)):
        L[i] += 5

n = int(input())
L = [int(input()) for _ in range(n)]
add_five(L)
print(L)
activity.hint: Change L[i] inside a loop over range(len(L)).

options: B is an alias of A
quiz.why: B = A does not copy the list. B and A refer to the same list object, so B is an alias of A.
A[:] is a slice of the whole list, and it makes a new copy. B = A only makes another name for the same list.
M[0] is [1, 2], and its element at index 1 is 2.

quiz.q: A list changed inside a function…
quiz.why: A list passed to a function is not copied, so changes made inside the function change the original list too, as it is mutable.
copy() makes a new list object, so id(A) and id(B) differ and the comparison is False.

lessons.title: List programs: search, frequency and more

scenes.text: Riya searches a list of roll numbers for 27.
She also counts how many students scored above 80.
These patterns appear in every exam.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Linear search
Solved example 2: Count above a value
steps.body: marks = [78, 85, 92, 66, 81]; count = sum(1 for m in marks if m > 80) → **3**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: Separate evens and odds
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Returning −1 inside the loop on the first mismatch (must be after the loop).
- Modifying a list while iterating over it with for x in L.

activity.prompt: Read n, then n integers (one per line), then a key. Print the index of the first occurrence of the key using linear search, or -1 if absent.
activity.starter:
n = int(input())
L = [int(input()) for _ in range(n)]
key = int(input())

quiz.q: If not found, our search returns…
quiz.why: By convention, a search function returns −1 when the item is not found, since −1 is not a valid index.
The list comprehension keeps only values greater than 2, so the result is [3, 4].

quiz.q: Worst case comparisons for linear search in n elements:
quiz.why: In the worst case (the item is last or absent), linear search compares all n elements, so n comparisons.
sum() adds the items of the list: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

questions.q: Lists are enclosed in…
questions.why: Lists are written inside square brackets [ ].

questions.q: Lists are…
questions.why: Lists are mutable, so their elements can be changed after creation.
append adds the element 4 at the end, so L becomes [1, 2, 3, 4].
A nested list counts as a single element. The list [1, [2, 3], 4] has 3 elements.
sort() puts the list in ascending order in place, so L becomes [3, 5, 8].
insert(1, 15) puts 15 at index 1, shifting the rest right. So L = [10, 15, 20, 30].

questions.q: Assertion (A): L.sort() changes L but sorted(L) does not. Reason (R): sort() works in place while sorted() returns a new list.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. sort() changes the list in place, whereas sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves L alone.
L[1:4] takes indexes 1, 2, 3, which are 2, 3, 4.

questions.q: Output: A = [1, 2]; B = A; B.append(3); print(A)
questions.why: B = A makes B an alias for the same list. So B.append(3) also changes A, giving [1, 2, 3].

questions.q: Output: L = [1, 2, 3]; L.extend([4, 5]); print(len(L))
questions.why: extend adds each item of [4, 5] to L, so L gets 2 more elements. len(L) = 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.q: Output: L = [4, 7, 4, 9]; L.remove(4); print(L)
questions.why: remove(4) deletes only the first 4, so [4, 7, 4, 9] becomes [7, 4, 9].

questions.q: Output: L = [3, 1, 2]; print(L.pop(0) + L.pop())
questions.why: L.pop(0) removes 3, leaving [1, 2]. Then L.pop() removes 2. So 3 + 2 = 5.
M[1][0] is 3 and M[0][1] is 2. Their product is 6.

questions.q: Case: L = L.sort() was written. What is L now?
questions.why: sort() sorts in place and returns None. So L = L.sort() makes L equal to None.

questions.q: Output: L = [1, 2, 3]; print(L * 2 == L + L)
questions.why: L * 2 repeats the list, and L + L joins the list with itself. Both give [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3], so they are equal.
L[1:3] = [5] replaces the two elements 20 and 30 with one element, 5. So L becomes [10, 5, 40].

questions.q: Output: def f(L): L = [0]; A = [1, 2]; f(A); print(A)
questions.why: Inside the function, L = [0] points the local name L to a new list. The caller's list A is not changed, so A stays [1, 2].

story.title: A record that should not change

scenes.text: Riya stores her date of birth as (12, 5, 2010).
It should never be changed by mistake.
A tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence.

steps.title: Creating tuples
steps.body: Elements in parentheses separated by commas: t = (1, 2, 3); mixed = (1, "a", 2.5); empty = (); **single element needs a comma**: (5,) is a tuple, (5) is just the integer 5. Parentheses are optional: t = 1, 2, 3 (tuple packing). tuple("abc") → ('a', 'b', 'c').

steps.title: Indexing and immutability
steps.body: Indexing and slicing work like lists: t[0], t[−1], t[1:3]. But elements cannot be changed: t[0] = 9 → **TypeError**. A tuple can contain a mutable list whose contents can change: t = (1, [2, 3]); t[1].append(4) → (1, [2, 3, 4]).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: type((5)) → int; type((5,)) → tuple.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the comma in single-element tuples.
- Trying to append to a tuple.

activity.prompt: Read three integers (separate lines), store them in a tuple, and print the tuple and then its reverse (as a tuple) on two lines.
activity.starter:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
c = int(input())
activity.solution:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
c = int(input())
t = (a, b, c)
print(t)
print(t[::-1])
activity.hint: Slicing with [::-1] reverses a tuple too.

quiz.why: A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma. (5,) is a tuple, while (5) is just the integer 5.
Tuples are immutable, so their items cannot be changed after creation.
t[−1] is the last element, so for (4, 5, 6) it is 6.
Tuples are immutable, so assigning to an item, as t[0] = 1, raises a TypeError.
tuple('hi') makes a tuple of the characters, ('h', 'i').

lessons.title: Tuple operations, methods and tuple assignment

scenes.text: Riya receives a tuple (name, class, roll) from a function.
She unpacks it into three variables in one line.
Tuples also support counting, searching and sorting.

steps.title: Operations and methods
steps.body: Concatenation (1, 2) + (3,) → (1, 2, 3); repetition (0,) * 3 → (0, 0, 0); membership; slicing. Methods/functions: len(), count(x), index(x), sorted(t) (returns a **list**), min(), max(), sum().

steps.title: Tuple assignment (unpacking)
steps.body: name, cls, roll = ("Riya", 11, 27) → name = "Riya", cls = 11, roll = 27. Number of variables must equal number of elements (else ValueError). Swap: a, b = b, a uses tuples. Functions return multiple values as tuples.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Nested tuple
steps.body: students = (("Riya", 92), ("Arjun", 85)); for name, m in students: print(name, m) → Riya 92 / Arjun 85.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting sorted(t) to return a tuple (it returns a list).
- Unpacking with the wrong number of variables.

activity.prompt: Read n, then n integers (one per line). Store them in a tuple and print the maximum, minimum and sum on one line separated by spaces.
activity.starter:
n = int(input())
t = tuple(int(input()) for _ in range(n))
activity.solution:
n = int(input())
t = tuple(int(input()) for _ in range(n))
print(max(t), min(t), sum(t))
activity.hint: Use max(), min() and sum() on the tuple.

quiz.why: The + operator joins tuples. (1, 2) + (3,) = (1, 2, 3).
sorted() always returns a list, even if the input is a tuple. So the result is [1, 2, 3].
a, b = (5, 6) unpacks the tuple so a = 5 and b = 6.
The value 2 appears twice in (2, 2, 3), so count(2) = 2.
There are 3 values but only 2 variables to unpack into. This raises a ValueError (too many values to unpack).

scenes.text: Riya stores friends’ numbers: {"Asha": 98765, "Ravi": 91234}.
She looks up a number by name, not by position.
She can add or change entries any time.

steps.title: Creating and accessing
steps.body: A **dictionary** is a mutable collection of **key: value** pairs in braces: d = {"Asha": 98765, "Ravi": 91234}. Keys must be **unique** and **immutable** (str, int, tuple); values can be anything. Access by key: d["Asha"] → 98765; missing key → **KeyError**; d.get("Zoya") → None (or a default: d.get("Zoya", 0)). Since Python 3.7, dictionaries keep insertion order.

steps.title: Adding, modifying, deleting
steps.body: d["Zoya"] = 99001 (adds); d["Ravi"] = 90000 (modifies); del d["Asha"] (deletes); d.pop("Ravi") (removes and returns value). Membership checks **keys**: "Zoya" in d → True.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: marks = {"Maths": 90, "CS": 95}; marks["Eco"] = 88 → {'Maths': 90, 'CS': 95, 'Eco': 88}; marks["Maths"] += 2 → 92.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: d = {1: "one", 2: "two"}; 2 in d → True; "two" in d → False (values are not checked).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a list as a key (unhashable → TypeError).
- Expecting in to search values.
- Accessing a missing key with [] instead of get().

activity.prompt: Create a dictionary of marks {"Maths": 90, "CS": 95}. Read a subject name and marks (separate lines), add or update that subject, then print the dictionary.
activity.solution:
marks = {"Maths": 90, "CS": 95}
sub = input()
m = int(input())
marks[sub] = m
print(marks)
activity.hint: Assigning d[key] = value adds or updates.

quiz.why: A dictionary stores key: value pairs.
Dictionary keys must be unique and immutable (hashable), such as strings, numbers or tuples. Lists cannot be keys.
Assigning to a new key adds a new key–value pair. So key 'b' is added with value 2.

quiz.q: d.get("x") for a missing key returns…
quiz.why: get() returns None if the key is missing, instead of raising a KeyError.
The 'in' operator on a dictionary checks the keys, not the values.

scenes.text: Riya’s marks are in a dictionary.
She loops through to print each subject and total.
Methods like keys(), values() and items() help.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: len(d) · d.keys() · d.values() · d.items() (pairs) · d.get(k, default) · d.update(other) (merge/overwrite) · d.pop(k) · d.popitem() (last inserted) · d.clear() · dict(list_of_pairs) · dict.fromkeys(keys, value) · sorted(d) (sorted keys) · min/max/sum on keys or values.

steps.title: Traversal
Solved example 1
steps.body: d = {"Maths": 92, "CS": 95, "Eco": 88}; list(d.keys()) → ['Maths', 'CS', 'Eco']; sum(d.values()) → 275; max(d, key=d.get) → 'CS'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing dictionary size while iterating over it.
- Forgetting that update() overwrites existing keys.

activity.prompt: Read n, then n lines each with a subject and marks separated by a space (e.g. CS 95). Store them in a dictionary and print the total marks and the subject with the highest marks on two lines.
activity.hint: split() each line into subject and marks; track the key with the largest value.

quiz.why: items() returns all the key–value pairs of the dictionary.
len() of a dictionary is the number of keys (pairs). Here there are 2.
update() with an existing key overwrites its value. Keys are unique, so no duplicate is added.
values() gives 3 and 4, and sum adds them to 7.

quiz.q: for k in d loops over…
quiz.why: A for loop over a dictionary goes through its keys.

scenes.text: Riya wants to know how many times each letter appears in “banana”.
A dictionary is perfect: letter → count.
Frequency counting is a top exam program.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Character frequency
Solved example 2: Word count
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing freq[ch] += 1 without initialising (KeyError).
- Mixing up keys and values when printing.

activity.prompt: Read a word and print each distinct character with its count, one per line in order of first appearance, as "char count".
activity.hint: Use freq.get(ch, 0) + 1 to count; dictionaries keep insertion order.

quiz.why: freq.get(ch, 0) gives the default value 0 when ch is not already a key. That makes counting easy.
dict() can build a dictionary from a list of (key, value) pairs, giving {'a': 1, 'b': 2}.
The letter 'a' appears three times in 'banana', so the count is 3.

quiz.q: Insertion order in dict is kept from Python…
quiz.why: Dictionaries remember insertion order, and this became a language guarantee from Python 3.7.
freq[ch] += 1 reads the existing value first. If ch is not yet a key, it raises a KeyError.

questions.q: A tuple is…
questions.why: A tuple is immutable. Its items cannot be changed once it is made.

questions.q: Dictionary is written with…
questions.why: A dictionary is written inside curly braces { }.

questions.q: type((7,)) is…
questions.why: (7,) has a trailing comma, so it is a tuple. Without the comma, (7) would be an int.
d['a'] looks up the key 'a' and gives its value, 1.

questions.q: Dictionary keys must be…
questions.why: Dictionary keys must be immutable (hashable). Lists, which are mutable, cannot be used as keys.
index(2) gives the position of the first 2. In (1, 2, 3, 2) it is at index 1.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A list cannot be a dictionary key. Reason (R): Keys must be immutable (hashable).
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. A list is mutable and not hashable, so it cannot be a dictionary key.

questions.q: Output: d = {"x": 1, "y": 2}; print("y" in d, 2 in d)
questions.why: The 'in' operator tests keys. 'y' is a key (True), while 2 is a value and not a key (False).

questions.q: Output: t = (5, 1, 4); print(sorted(t))
questions.why: sorted() returns a list, even for a tuple. So the result is [1, 4, 5].

questions.q: Output: d = {}; d["a"] = d.get("a", 0) + 1; d["a"] = d.get("a", 0) + 1; print(d)
questions.why: d.get('a', 0) + 1 adds 1 to the current count. Doing it twice makes the count 2, so d = {'a': 2}.

questions.q: Output: a, b, c = "xyz"; print(b)
questions.why: A string can be unpacked into its characters. a, b, c = 'xyz' gives a = 'x', b = 'y', c = 'z'.

questions.q: Output: d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}; d.update({"b": 5, "c": 3}); print(sum(d.values()))
questions.why: update changes b to 5 and adds c = 3. The values are 1, 5, 3, and their sum is 9.

questions.q: Output: t = (1, [2, 3]); t[1].append(4); print(t)
questions.why: The tuple itself cannot change, but the list inside it is mutable. So append(4) works and t becomes (1, [2, 3, 4]).

questions.q: Case: A program needs to store each roll number with a name and look up names quickly by roll number. Best structure?
questions.why: A dictionary with roll numbers as keys and names as values gives quick lookup of a name by its roll number.

questions.q: Output: d = {1: "a", 2: "b"}; print(d.pop(1), len(d))
questions.why: pop(1) removes key 1 and returns its value 'a'. One pair is left, so len(d) = 1. The output is a 1.

questions.q: Output: print(len(dict.fromkeys("hello")))
questions.why: dict.fromkeys('hello') makes keys from the characters, and duplicate keys merge. The distinct keys are h, e, l, o, so the length is 4.

questions.q: Which statement raises an error?
questions.why: A tuple does not support item assignment, so t[0] = 5 raises a TypeError. The other statements are valid.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Societal Impact
courses.summary: Digital footprints, net and social-media etiquette, intellectual property and its violations, open licences (CC, GPL, Apache), cyber crimes and safety (with Indian helplines), the IT Act 2000 and DPDP Act 2023, e-waste management and health impacts of technology.
outcomes: Learners can explain digital footprints and practise netiquette
Learners can distinguish copyright, patent, trademark and open licences
Learners can recognise cyber crimes and respond safely
Learners can describe India’s IT and data laws, e-waste rules and healthy tech habits

lessons.title: Digital footprints and being a good netizen

story.title: The photo that never went away

scenes.text: Kabir posts a silly photo at 15; years later a recruiter finds it.
Websites also record what he searches and where he clicks.
Everything we do online leaves a trail — a digital footprint.

steps.title: Digital footprints
steps.body:
Data trail left by our online activity.

- **Active footprint**: data we intentionally share — posts, comments, emails, form entries.
- **Passive footprint**: data collected without our direct input — browsing history, cookies, location, IP address, app usage.

Footprints are hard to delete fully; they can be used for advertising, profiling, or misuse.

steps.title: Net etiquette (netiquette)
steps.body:
- **Be ethical**: no copyright violation; share expertise.
- **Be respectful**: respect privacy; respect diversity; no trolling.
- **Be responsible**: avoid cyber bullying; do not feed trolls; think before you post.

**Communication etiquette** (email, chat): be precise, polite, use appropriate subject lines, avoid ALL CAPS (shouting), respect others’ time and privacy (BCC when needed).
**Social media etiquette**: choose strong passwords, know who you befriend, beware of fake information, think before uploading, use privacy settings.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Active or passive?
steps.body: A comment you post → active. A shopping site recording products you viewed → passive. Location tagged automatically on a photo → passive (unless you chose it).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Reduce your footprint
steps.body: Review privacy settings, turn off location tags, clear cookies, avoid sharing phone numbers and school details publicly, use separate emails for sign-ups.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing deleted posts are gone forever (screenshots and backups exist).
- Thinking “private” accounts make everything safe.

activity.prompt: Active or passive digital footprint?

items.text: IP address logged by a site

quiz.q: Browsing history collected by sites is…
quiz.why: Data collected about you without your direct input, like browsing history, is a passive digital footprint.

quiz.q: Typing in ALL CAPS online is seen as…
quiz.why: Typing in ALL CAPS online is considered shouting and is bad netiquette.
A good netizen respects the privacy and diversity of others, and follows netiquette.
Digital footprints stay online for a long time and copies may exist, so they are hard to erase completely.
A strong password mixes uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols, and is not shared or easy to guess.

lessons.title: Intellectual property, plagiarism and open licences

scenes.text: Riya’s classmate copies an article into his project and puts his own name on it.
That is plagiarism — and may infringe copyright.
Some creators share work under open licences that allow reuse with credit.

steps.title: Intellectual Property Rights (IPR)
steps.body:
- **Copyright**: protects original creative works (books, music, software code, films) — automatically on creation; others need permission to copy/distribute.
- **Patent**: protects inventions; exclusive rights for a fixed term (20 years in India) in exchange for public disclosure.
- **Trademark**: protects brand names, logos, slogans that distinguish goods/services.

steps.title: Violations
steps.body:
- **Plagiarism**: presenting someone else’s work or ideas as your own without credit.
- **Copyright infringement**: using copyrighted work without permission (pirated software, movies).
- **Trademark infringement**: unauthorised use of another’s mark or a confusingly similar one.

steps.title: Public access and open source licences
steps.body:
- **Creative Commons (CC)**: lets creators allow reuse with conditions — attribution (BY), share-alike (SA), non-commercial (NC), no derivatives (ND).
- **GNU General Public License (GPL)**: free software licence; modified versions must also be released under GPL (copyleft).
- **Apache License**: permissive; allows use, modification and distribution, including in proprietary software, with notices.
- Examples of FOSS: Linux, LibreOffice, Python, Firefox, GIMP.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the issue
steps.body: (a) Using a pirated copy of paid software → copyright infringement. (b) Copying paragraphs from a website without citing → plagiarism. (c) A local shop naming itself “Adiddas” with a similar logo → trademark infringement.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Using a CC image
steps.body: An image licensed CC BY-SA can be used in your blog if you give credit and share your adapted version under the same licence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking anything on the internet is free to use.
- Believing changing a few words avoids plagiarism.

activity.prompt: Match the term
pairs: Protects original creative works like code and music
Protects inventions for a fixed period
Passing off others’ work as your own
Flexible licences like BY, SA, NC, ND

quiz.why: Using someone else's text without giving credit is plagiarism.
A patent protects inventions. Brand names are protected by trademarks and novels by copyright.
The Creative Commons licence CC BY allows use of the work if you give attribution (credit) to the creator.
Using pirated (unlicensed copied) software breaks the owner's rights, so it is copyright infringement.
Linux is free and open-source software (FOSS), whose source code is open for everyone.

scenes.text: An SMS says: “Your bank account will be blocked. Click here to update KYC.”
The link leads to a fake site that steals passwords — phishing.
Knowing common cyber crimes helps you stay safe.

steps.title: Common cyber crimes
steps.body:
- **Hacking**: unauthorised access to computers or networks (*ethical hacking* is authorised security testing).
- **Phishing**: fake emails/SMS/websites to steal passwords, OTPs, card details.
- **Identity theft**: using someone’s personal information to impersonate them (loans, fake accounts).
- **Ransomware**: malware that encrypts data and demands payment.
- **Cyber bullying**: harassing, threatening or humiliating someone online (posting rumours, sharing private images, exclusion).
- **Online fraud, cyber stalking, spreading malware (viruses, worms, Trojans)**.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body: Use strong unique passwords and two-factor authentication; never share OTP/PIN; verify URLs (https and correct domain); update software and antivirus; back up data; avoid unknown downloads; use privacy settings; log out on shared devices; think before clicking.

steps.title: If it happens to you
steps.body:
- Do not panic or pay ransom; disconnect the device.
- Save evidence (screenshots, links, messages).
- Report on the **National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in)** or call the **cybercrime helpline 1930**; tell a trusted adult/teacher.
- For bullying: do not reply angrily; block and report; talk to someone you trust. Childline **1098**, emergency **112**, Tele-MANAS mental-health helpline **14416**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the crime
steps.body: (a) Fake bank SMS asking for OTP → phishing. (b) Files locked with a demand for bitcoin → ransomware. (c) Someone opens a social media account in your name → identity theft. (d) Classmates repeatedly post mocking memes about a student → cyber bullying.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Spot a fake URL
steps.body: www.sbi.co.in (genuine domain) vs www.sbi-kyc-update.com (suspicious) — check spelling, domain and https; banks never ask for OTP by SMS links.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharing an OTP with someone claiming to be bank staff.
- Staying silent about cyber bullying — reporting helps you and others.

a.text: A classmate shares an edited, embarrassing photo of you in a group chat and others laugh. What do you do first?

choices.label: Post something hurtful back
choices.feedback: Retaliation usually makes it worse and can get you in trouble too.

choices.label: Save screenshots, block/report, and tell a trusted adult
choices.feedback: Evidence + support is the right first step.

b.text: The fight grows. Step back: you can still save evidence and ask for help.

choices.label: Save evidence and tell a teacher/parent

c.text: The adult helps report it to the platform and school. If threats continue, it can be reported at cybercrime.gov.in or 1930.

end.text: You are not alone. If you feel low or anxious, you can call Tele-MANAS 14416 anytime.

quiz.q: A fake email asking for your password is…
quiz.why: A fake email that tries to trick you into giving a password is phishing.

quiz.q: Malware that locks files for payment is…
quiz.why: Ransomware is malware that locks or encrypts files and asks for a payment to unlock them.
The national cybercrime helpline number in India is 1930.
Two-factor authentication adds a second check beyond the password, so it makes accounts safer. Sharing OTPs or reusing passwords is unsafe.

options: save evidence and tell a trusted adult
quiz.why: If someone is cyber-bullied, they should save the evidence (screenshots) and tell a trusted adult, who can help report it.

lessons.title: Indian IT Act, data protection, e-waste and health

scenes.text: India has laws for electronic records, cyber crimes and personal data.
Old phones and laptops become toxic e-waste if dumped.
Long screen time affects eyes, posture and sleep.

steps.title: Indian IT Act and data protection
steps.body:
- **Information Technology Act, 2000** (amended **2008**): gives legal recognition to electronic records and **digital signatures**; defines cyber crimes and penalties (e.g., hacking, identity theft, publishing obscene material); provides for adjudicating officers and an appellate tribunal.
- **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**: rules for processing personal data; requires consent and purpose limitation; gives individuals rights (access, correction, erasure, grievance redress); special care for children’s data.
- This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: E-waste management
steps.body:
**E-waste**: discarded electronic devices (phones, computers, batteries, TVs). Contains toxic substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium that pollute soil and water if dumped or burnt.

Management: **reduce** (buy only what you need), **reuse** (repair, donate, resell), **recycle** at authorised e-waste recyclers/collection centres. India has **E-Waste (Management) Rules** with extended producer responsibility for manufacturers.

steps.title: Impact on health
steps.body:
- **Eye strain** (dry eyes, blurred vision) → follow the 20-20-20 rule (every 20 minutes look 20 feet away for 20 seconds).
- **Musculoskeletal problems** (neck, back, wrist) → good **ergonomics**: screen at eye level, back support, feet flat, wrists straight.
- **Sleep problems** and **internet/gaming addiction** → screen-time limits, no screens before bed, offline hobbies.
- If anxiety, low mood or compulsive use persists, talk to a trusted adult or a professional (Tele-MANAS 14416).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Which law?
steps.body: A company collects students’ phone numbers for ads without consent → issue under the **DPDP Act, 2023**. Someone hacks a school server → offence under the **IT Act, 2000**. A contract signed with a digital signature → valid under the **IT Act**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Old phone
steps.body: Instead of throwing an old phone in the dustbin: wipe data, remove SIM/memory card, then donate, sell or give to an authorised e-waste collector.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Throwing batteries and phones in normal garbage.
- Thinking the IT Act covers only hacking (it also gives legal status to e-records and digital signatures).

activity.prompt: Healthy and responsible tech habits
items: Keep the screen at eye level and sit upright
Wipe data before giving away a device
Give old electronics to an authorised e-waste collector
Never share others’ personal data without consent

quiz.q: The IT Act of India was passed in…
quiz.why: The Information Technology Act of India was passed in 2000, and was amended in 2008.
The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, deals with protection of personal data.
E-waste contains toxic substances such as lead and mercury, which harm health and the environment if not handled properly.
The 20-20-20 rule is: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. It helps reduce eye strain.

quiz.q: The IT Act gives legal recognition to…
quiz.why: The IT Act gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures.

questions.q: Browsing history is a…
questions.why: Browsing history is collected without you entering it deliberately, so it is a passive digital footprint.

questions.q: Phishing aims to…
questions.why: Phishing aims to steal sensitive information such as passwords and card details by tricking people.

questions.q: India’s IT Act was enacted in…
questions.why: India's Information Technology Act was enacted in 2000.

questions.q: Presenting others’ work as your own is…
questions.why: Presenting someone else's work as your own is plagiarism.

questions.q: Which licence is copyleft?
questions.why: The GNU General Public License (GPL) is a copyleft licence, which requires derived work to be shared under the same terms.

questions.q: E-waste should be…
questions.why: E-waste has toxic materials, so it should be given to authorised recyclers and not buried, burnt or dumped.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Netizens should not share others’ photos without consent. Reason (R): Respecting privacy is part of net etiquette.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Respecting others' privacy is part of netiquette, so one should not share their photos without consent.

questions.q: Case: A message says “You won a lottery, pay ₹500 processing fee.” This is likely…
questions.why: A message that says you won a lottery and asks you to pay a fee is a typical online scam, which is a kind of fraud or phishing.

questions.q: Case: Files encrypted with a ransom note. Best first step?
options: Share the note on social media
questions.why: With ransomware, do not pay. Disconnect the device from the network, and report to 1930 or the cybercrime portal. Paying does not guarantee getting files back.

questions.q: Which is a trademark?
questions.why: A trademark protects a brand identity such as a logo or name. Inventions are protected by patents and songs and novels by copyright.

questions.q: Case: A student uses a CC BY image in a project and credits the creator. This is…
questions.why: A CC BY licence allows use with attribution. Using the image and crediting the creator follows the licence, so it is legal use.

questions.q: DPDP Act 2023 gives individuals rights such as…
options: access, correction and erasure of personal data
questions.why: The DPDP Act 2023 gives individuals rights over their personal data, such as the right to access, correct and erase it.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ethical hacking is legal. Reason (R): It is authorised testing to find security weaknesses.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Ethical hacking is done with permission, to find and fix security weaknesses, so it is legal.

questions.q: Case: Someone creates a social media profile with your photos and name to cheat others. Crime?
questions.why: Making a fake profile using your photos and name to cheat others is identity theft (impersonation).

questions.q: Which ergonomic practice is correct?
options: Sitting without back support for hours
Screen at eye level, back supported
questions.why: Good ergonomics means the screen is at eye level and the back is supported. Poor posture can cause neck, back and wrist problems.

questions.q: Case: A school app shares students’ data with advertisers without consent. Which law is most relevant?
questions.why: Sharing students' personal data with advertisers without consent is covered by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

questions.q: Case: A company uses Apache-licensed code inside its paid product and keeps notices. Is it allowed?
questions.why: The Apache licence is permissive. It lets a company use the code in a paid product if it keeps the required notices, and it need not release its own code.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 11 Computer Science
courses.summary: Python quick reference, theory quick sheet for systems, number systems, emerging trends and societal impact, output-prediction and debugging drills, and two mixed mock papers.
outcomes: Learners can recall Python syntax and common traps
Learners can revise all theory chapters quickly
Learners can predict outputs and fix errors
Learners can attempt full mock papers

scenes.text: Exam tomorrow — Riya wants all Python syntax on one page.
Data types, operators, loops, strings, lists, tuples, dictionaries.
Here it is, followed by a practice program.

steps.title: Basics and operators
steps.body: input() → str; int(), float(), str(). Arithmetic + − * / // % **; relational == != < > <= >=; logical and or not; membership in; identity is. Precedence: () > ** > unary − > * / // % > + − > relational > not > and > or. ** is right-associative.

steps.title: Control flow
steps.body: if / elif / else with colon and indentation. for x in range(start, stop, step) (stop excluded). while cond:. break exits loop; continue skips iteration; pass placeholder; loop else runs if no break.

steps.title: Strings, lists, tuples, dicts
steps.body:
Strings: immutable; s[i], s[a:b:c], len, upper, lower, title, find (−1), count, replace, split, join, strip, isdigit, isalpha.
Lists: mutable; append, extend, insert, remove, pop, sort (None), sorted (new), reverse, count, index; aliasing B = A vs copy A[:].
Tuples: immutable; (x,) single; unpacking; count, index.
Dicts: {key: value}; keys immutable and unique; d[k], d.get(k, default), keys(), values(), items(), update, pop, del; in checks keys.

steps.title: Functions and modules
steps.body: def f(a, b=2): return …; default parameters last; keyword arguments; global keyword; import math (sqrt, ceil, floor, pi, gcd, factorial); random (random, randint inclusive, randrange); statistics (mean, median, mode).

steps.title: Top traps
steps.body: 7 / 2 = 3.5; −7 // 2 = −4; (5) is int; L = L.sort() makes None; strings cannot be changed in place; range(1, 10) excludes 10; "a" in dict checks keys.

activity.prompt: Read a line of space-separated integers. Print the count of even numbers and the count of odd numbers on one line separated by a space.
activity.hint: Loop through the list and test n % 2.

quiz.why: // is floor division, which rounds down toward −∞. −7/2 = −3.5, and its floor is −4.
range(2, 8, 2) starts at 2 and goes up by 2, stopping before 8: 2, 4, 6.
find returns −1 if the text is not found. 'z' is not in 'abc'.
sort() sorts the list in place and returns None.
get('x', 0) returns the default 0 when the key 'x' is missing.

lessons.title: Theory quick sheet: systems, numbers, trends, society

scenes.text: About a third of the paper is theory.
Memory units, conversions, gates, software types, emerging trends and cyber safety.
Revise them here.

steps.title: Computer system
steps.body: CPU = ALU + CU + registers. Memory: registers > cache > RAM (volatile) > secondary; ROM non-volatile. 1 KB = 1024 B … Buses: data (bi), address (uni), control. Microprocessor vs microcontroller. Software: system (OS, utilities, drivers), translators (assembler, compiler, interpreter), applications (general, customised), proprietary vs FOSS. OS functions: process, memory, file, device management. Gates: NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR; De Morgan’s laws.

steps.title: Number systems
steps.body: Decimal → base b: repeated division (read remainders bottom-up); fraction: repeated multiplication (top-down). Base b → decimal: positional values. Binary ↔ octal: groups of 3; binary ↔ hex: groups of 4. ASCII 7-bit (A = 65, a = 97, 0 = 48); ISCII 8-bit; Unicode (UTF-8/16/32).

steps.title: Emerging trends
steps.body: AI, ML (learns from data), NLP, VR vs AR, robotics, big data 5 Vs, IoT/WoT, sensors, smart cities, cloud (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), grid computing, blockchain (hash-linked distributed ledger).

steps.title: Societal impact
steps.body: Active/passive footprints; netiquette; copyright/patent/trademark; plagiarism; CC, GPL (copyleft), Apache (permissive); phishing, hacking, ransomware, identity theft, cyber bullying; IT Act 2000 (2008); DPDP Act 2023; e-waste; health (20-20-20, ergonomics). Helplines: 1930, 112, 1098, 14416.

steps.title: Classic mix-ups
steps.body: Compiler (whole program) vs interpreter (line by line) · address bus unidirectional · VR replaces, AR adds · GPL copyleft vs Apache permissive · ASCII 7-bit vs ISCII 8-bit.

cards.back: Platform to deploy apps without managing servers

quiz.why: The address bus is unidirectional, as the CPU sends addresses to memory. The data bus is bidirectional.
Online email is software given as a service over the internet, so it is SaaS.
The cybercrime helpline in India is 1930.
An interpreter translates and runs a program line by line, as Python does.

scenes.text: Board papers love “find the output” and “correct the errors” questions.
Trace slowly, write variable values in a table.
Practise here, then try the mocks.

steps.title: Trace 1
steps.body:
x = 3
for i in range(1, 4):
    x = x * i
print(x)
Trace: i=1 → 3; i=2 → 6; i=3 → 18 → **18**.

steps.title: Trace 2
steps.body:
s = "PYTHON"
print(s[1:5:2], s[-2:])
Indices 1, 3 → "YH"; last two "ON" → **YH ON**.

steps.title: Trace 3
steps.body:
L = [1, 2, 3]
M = L
M.append(4)
print(len(L), L[-1])
Alias → **4 4**.

steps.title: Debug 1
steps.body:
Faulty: for i in range(5)
    print(i)
Errors: missing colon after range(5). Fixed: for i in range(5):

steps.title: Debug 2
steps.body:
Faulty: n = input(); print(n + 5)
Error: TypeError (str + int). Fixed: n = int(input()); print(n + 5).

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Write a trace table (variables as columns, iterations as rows). Watch for stop-excluded ranges, integer vs float division, aliasing, and string immutability.

activity.prompt: Fix and complete: read a word and print it reversed in uppercase. (Hint: slicing and upper().)
activity.solution:
w = input()
print(w[::-1].upper())
activity.hint: Use w[::-1] and .upper().

quiz.why: ** comes before *. 3 ** 2 = 9, so 2 * 9 = 18.
'ab'[::−1] is 'ba'. Then 'ba' * 2 = 'baba'.
insert(0, 4) puts 4 at index 0, so L becomes [4, 5, 6].
A single = is assignment and is not allowed in a condition. The comparison operator is ==, so it should be if x == 5:.
(1, 2) + (3,) gives (1, 2, 3), which has length 3.

questions.q: [Mock A] RAM is…
questions.why: RAM is volatile memory, which loses its contents when the power is switched off.

questions.q: [Mock A] (1100)₂ in decimal:
[Mock A] Which is a valid identifier?
questions.why: _sum1 is valid, as it starts with an underscore and has only letters and digits. 'sum-1' has a hyphen, '1sum' starts with a digit and 'for' is a keyword.

questions.q: [Mock A] Output: print(17 // 5, 17 % 5)
questions.why: 17 // 5 = 3 and 17 % 5 = 2. The output is 3 2.

questions.q: [Mock A] (156)₁₀ in hex:
questions.why: 156 = 9 × 16 + 12, and 12 is C in hex. So (156)₁₀ = 9C.

questions.q: [Mock A] Assertion (A): 5 / 2 gives 2.5 in Python 3. Reason (R): The / operator always performs true (float) division.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. In Python 3, / always does true division and gives a float, so 5 / 2 = 2.5.

questions.q: [Mock A] Output: s = "Computer"; print(s[2:5])
questions.why: s[2:5] takes indexes 2, 3, 4 of 'Computer': m, p, u. So it gives 'mpu'.

questions.q: [Mock A] Output: L = [3, 1, 2]; L.sort(reverse=True); print(L)
questions.why: sort(reverse=True) sorts in descending order, so [3, 1, 2] becomes [3, 2, 1].

questions.q: [Mock A] Output: d = {"a": 2, "b": 3}; print(d["a"] * d.get("c", 4))
questions.why: d['a'] is 2 and d.get('c', 4) uses the default 4, since 'c' is missing. 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: An SMS asks you to click a link and enter your UPI PIN to receive cashback. This is…
questions.why: A message asking you to click a link and enter your UPI PIN to receive money is phishing. You never need a PIN to receive money.

questions.q: [Mock A] Output: x = 0; for i in range(1, 10, 3): x += i; print(x)
questions.why: range(1, 10, 3) gives 1, 4, 7. Their sum is 12.

questions.q: [Mock A] Output: print(len("Hello World".split()))
questions.why: split() with no argument splits on spaces, so 'Hello World' gives two words. The length is 2.

questions.q: [Mock B] A microcontroller is found in…
questions.why: A microcontroller is an embedded chip found in appliances such as microwave ovens. Supercomputers use powerful processors instead.

questions.q: [Mock B] GPL is…
questions.why: The GPL is a copyleft licence, since derived software must be shared under the same licence.

questions.q: [Mock B] (67)₈ in binary:
questions.why: Convert each octal digit to 3 bits: 6 = 110 and 7 = 111. So (67)₈ = 110111.

questions.q: [Mock B] Output: print(type((1)), type((1,)))
questions.why: (1) is just the integer 1 in brackets, so it is an int. (1,) has a comma, so it is a tuple.

questions.q: [Mock B] Output: def f(a, b=5): return a * b; print(f(2) + f(2, 1))
questions.why: f(2) uses b = 5, giving 10. f(2, 1) gives 2. Their sum is 12.

questions.q: [Mock B] XOR of 1 and 0 is…
questions.why: XOR gives 1 when the two inputs are different. For 1 and 0 the result is 1.

questions.q: [Mock B] Output: s = "level"; print(s == s[::-1], s.count("l"))
questions.why: 'level' reads the same backwards, so the comparison is True. The letter 'l' appears 2 times (first and last).

questions.q: [Mock B] Output: L = [1, 2, 3, 4]; print(L[::-1][1])
questions.why: L[::−1] is [4, 3, 2, 1]. Its element at index 1 is 3.

questions.q: [Mock B] Output: n = 1234; r = 0; while n: r = r * 10 + n % 10; n //= 10; print(r)
questions.why: The loop builds the reverse of the number by taking the last digit each time. 1234 gives 4321.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: Renting virtual servers and storage from a provider is…
questions.why: Renting virtual servers and storage is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

questions.q: [Mock B] Output: freq = {}; for c in "aab": freq[c] = freq.get(c, 0) + 1; print(freq)
questions.why: get(c, 0) + 1 counts each character. For 'aab', a is counted twice and b once, and the keys keep insertion order: {'a': 2, 'b': 1}.

questions.q: [Mock B] Output: print(sum(x * x for x in range(4)))
questions.why: The squares of 0, 1, 2, 3 are 0, 1, 4, 9. Their sum is 14.

school-c11-economics-a.title: Class 11 Economics (Part A)
school-c11-economics-a.description: Statistics for Economics and Indian Economic Development for Class 11, chapter by chapter, with solved numericals, case studies and tests.

courses.title: Statistics Ch 1 · Introduction
courses.summary: Why economics: scarcity, choice and economic activities; meaning of statistics in singular and plural senses; types of data and variables; importance and limitations of statistics in economics.
outcomes: Learners can explain scarcity and economic activities
Learners can define statistics in both senses
Learners can distinguish qualitative/quantitative and discrete/continuous data
Learners can explain uses and limitations of statistics

lessons.title: Why economics? Scarcity, choice and economic activities

scenes.text: Rohan has ₹500 a month but wants a cricket ball, a novel and movie tickets.
He cannot have everything — he must choose.
Economics studies how people make such choices.

steps.title: Wants, resources and scarcity
steps.body: Human wants are unlimited, while resources (money, time, land, labour) are limited and have alternative uses. This **scarcity** forces **choice**. Economics studies how individuals, firms and governments choose to use scarce resources to satisfy wants.

steps.title: Economic agents and activities
steps.body:
- **Consumer**: buys goods/services for personal use.
- **Producer**: makes goods/services for sale.
- **Service-holder/seller of services** and **saver/investor**.

Main economic activities:
- **Consumption**: using goods and services to satisfy wants.
- **Production**: creating goods and services.
- **Distribution**: dividing national income among factors as rent, wages, interest and profit.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify the activity
steps.body: (a) A farmer growing wheat → production. (b) Your family eating the bread → consumption. (c) The landowner receiving rent and the worker receiving wages → distribution of income.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Scarcity in action
steps.body: A village panchayat has ₹10 lakh and must choose between a school building and a road. Choosing the school means the road is given up — scarcity makes choice and sacrifice unavoidable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying scarcity means “very little exists” — it means *limited relative to wants*.
- Confusing distribution (of income) with distribution of goods by shops.

activity.prompt: Consumption, production or distribution?

quiz.q: The basic economic problem arises from…
options: scarcity of resources relative to wants
quiz.why: The basic economic problem arises from scarcity: resources are limited, but human wants are unlimited.

quiz.q: Using goods to satisfy wants is…
quiz.why: Using goods and services to satisfy wants is consumption.

quiz.q: Rent, wages, interest and profit relate to…
quiz.why: Rent, wages, interest and profit are the incomes of the factors of production, so they belong to distribution.
Resources have alternative uses, so using them for one purpose means giving up other uses. That is why choice is needed.
Because resources are scarce and wants are many, people and societies are forced to make choices.

sources: NCERT Statistics for Economics Class 11 — topic reference

lessons.title: Meaning of statistics: singular and plural

scenes.text: A newspaper says, “Average monthly rainfall in Kerala in July is about 650 mm.”
That number is a statistic — and the method used to get it is statistics.
The word has two meanings.

steps.title: Plural sense: statistical data
steps.body: Statistics (plural) are **numerical facts** that are: aggregates of facts (not single figures), affected by multiple causes, numerically expressed, enumerated or estimated with reasonable accuracy, collected systematically for a predetermined purpose, and placed in relation to each other (comparable).

steps.title: Singular sense: statistical methods
steps.body:
Statistics (singular) is the **science** of collection, organisation, presentation, analysis and interpretation of numerical data.

- Collection → Organisation → Presentation → Analysis → Interpretation.

steps.title: Quantitative and qualitative data
steps.body:
- **Quantitative**: measurable in numbers (income, height, marks).
- **Qualitative**: attributes not directly measurable (gender, honesty, colour, literacy status); can be counted by category.
- **Variable**: a characteristic that changes — *discrete* (whole values: number of children) or *continuous* (any value in a range: height, weight).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Is it statistics (data)?
steps.body: (a) “Ram’s height is 165 cm” → not statistics (single fact). (b) “Average height of 500 students is 162 cm” → statistics (aggregate, numerical, comparable). (c) “Indian cricketers are great” → not statistics (not numerical).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Discrete or continuous?
steps.body: Number of cars in a parking lot → discrete. Time taken to run 100 m → continuous. Number of rooms in a house → discrete. Temperature → continuous.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a single number “statistics”.
- Calling height a discrete variable because we round it.
- Forgetting that qualitative data can still be counted (e.g., number of literates).

activity.prompt: Discrete or continuous variable?

items.text: Number of students in a class

quiz.q: Statistics in the plural sense means…
quiz.why: In the plural sense, statistics means numerical data (facts expressed in numbers).
Religion is a quality that cannot be measured in numbers, so it is a qualitative characteristic (an attribute). Age, income and height are quantitative.

quiz.q: A single fact like “Asha scored 80” is…
quiz.why: A single figure such as 'Asha scored 80' is not an aggregate of facts, so it is not statistics.
Height can take any value in a range, such as 150.3 cm, so it is a continuous variable.

quiz.q: The first stage of statistical work is…
quiz.why: The first stage of statistical work is the collection of data. Then come organisation, presentation, analysis and interpretation.

lessons.title: Statistics in economics: importance and uses

scenes.text: The government wants to reduce unemployment.
It first measures how many people are unemployed, where, and in which age groups.
Without statistics, economic policy would be guesswork.

steps.title: What statistics does in economics
steps.body:
- **Presents facts precisely and definitely** (e.g., “inflation was 5%” rather than “prices rose”).
- **Condenses** mass data into a few measures (average, percentage).
- **Helps compare** across time and places.
- **Helps find relationships** between variables (price and demand, income and consumption).
- **Helps forecasting and policy formulation** (budget, monetary policy).
- **Tests economic laws/theories** with data.

steps.title: Uses for different groups
steps.body: **Government**: plans, budgets, poverty and employment estimates (e.g., surveys by the National Statistics Office). **Businesses**: demand forecasting, pricing, quality control. **Economists**: testing theories. **Individuals**: comparing prices, investments.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Which function?
steps.body: “Per-capita income rose from ₹X to ₹Y over 10 years” → comparison over time. “Average rainfall determines kharif output” → relationship between variables.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Policy use
steps.body: Data show high anaemia among adolescent girls in certain districts → targeted nutrition programmes there. Statistics guided *where* and *for whom*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating statistical results as certain truths — they are averages and estimates.
- Using data without checking how it was collected.

activity.prompt: Match the function of statistics

quiz.why: Statistics condenses large amounts of data into simple measures such as averages and percentages.

quiz.q: Studying price and demand together shows…
quiz.why: Studying price and demand together shows how the two are related, so it shows a relationship.
Governments use statistics for planning and policy making, since data show what is needed.
Statistical results are true on average, but not necessarily for every individual case.

quiz.q: Forecasting future demand is a function of…
quiz.why: Forecasting future demand uses past data and statistical methods, so it is a function of statistics.

scenes.text: An ad claims: “9 out of 10 dentists recommend our toothpaste!”
But they asked only 10 dentists, all paid by the company.
Statistics can mislead when misused.

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body:
- Studies **aggregates**, not individuals.
- Deals with **quantitative** facts; qualitative aspects need indirect measures.
- **Results are true on average**, not in every case.
- **Uniformity and homogeneity** of data are needed for comparison.
- Can be **misused** by people with vested interests.
- Should be used only by experts or with care.

steps.title: Ways statistics mislead
steps.body: Small or biased samples, wrong averages, missing base figures (“sales doubled” from 2 to 4 units), misleading graphs (truncated axes), comparing non-comparable data, confusing correlation with causation.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Spot the problem
steps.body: “Our profits grew 100%!” — from ₹1,000 to ₹2,000. True, but tiny base. Always ask: *percent of what?*

steps.title: Solved example 2: Averages hide things
steps.body: Average income of five people: ₹10,000, ₹12,000, ₹11,000, ₹9,000 and ₹5,08,000 = ₹1,10,000. The mean is unrepresentative; the median ₹11,000 is better here.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Accepting any percentage without the base.
- Comparing data collected with different definitions.
- Assuming correlation proves cause.

statements.s: Statistics studies individuals, not groups.
Statistical results are true on average.
A small biased sample can mislead.
A 100% rise always means a large increase.

quiz.why: Statistics deals mainly with aggregates (groups of facts), not with individual cases.
Mean = (10 + 12 + 11 + 9 + 508) ÷ 5 = 550 ÷ 5 = 110. The extreme value 508 pulls the mean up.

quiz.q: Better average for skewed income data is often…
quiz.why: For skewed data with extreme values, the median is a better average than the mean, as it is not much affected by extremes.
For data to be compared, they must be homogeneous, that is, of the same kind and defined in the same way.
A truncated axis, which does not start at zero, can make small differences look large. So it is a way to mislead with a graph.

questions.q: The basic economic problem is…
questions.why: The basic economic problem is scarcity, as resources are limited relative to wants.

questions.q: Payment of wages to workers relates to…
questions.why: Paying wages to workers is a share of income going to a factor of production, so it relates to distribution.

questions.q: Statistics in singular sense means…
questions.why: In the singular sense, statistics means the science or methods of collecting, organising, analysing and interpreting data.

questions.q: Which is a continuous variable?
questions.why: Weight can take any value within a range, so it is a continuous variable. The numbers of books, cars and rooms are counted in whole numbers, so they are discrete.

questions.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of statistics (data)?
questions.why: Statistics must be an aggregate of facts, so a single isolated figure is not a characteristic of statistics.

questions.q: Literacy status of a person is…
questions.why: Literacy status, such as literate or illiterate, is a quality and not a number, so it is qualitative.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Statistics does not study individuals. Reason (R): Statistics deals with aggregates of facts.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Statistics deals with aggregates of facts, so it does not study individuals separately.

questions.q: Arrange stages: (i) analysis (ii) collection (iii) presentation (iv) organisation (v) interpretation
questions.why: The stages of statistical work are collection (ii), organisation (iv), presentation (iii), analysis (i) and interpretation (v).

questions.q: Case: A firm says sales grew 200%, from 5 units to 15 units. Main issue?
options: Small base hides tiny absolute change
questions.why: Growing from 5 to 15 units is a 200% rise, but the actual change is just 10 units. A small base makes a small change look big.

questions.q: Income (₹ ‘000) of 5 people: 8, 9, 10, 11, 312. Mean?
In the case above, the most representative average is…
questions.why: The value 312 is an extreme value. The median (the middle value, 10) represents the typical income better than the mean of 70.

questions.q: Relationship between price and quantity demanded is studied using…
questions.why: The relationship between price and quantity demanded is studied with statistical methods such as correlation.

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE?
questions.why: Statistics can be misused, for example by choosing data selectively or using misleading graphs. The other statements are false.

questions.q: Case: A village survey records “number of members per household”. Variable type?
questions.why: The number of members in a household is counted in whole numbers (1, 2, 3 ...), so it is a discrete variable.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Statistics helps in policy formulation. Reason (R): Statistical data reveal the size and nature of economic problems.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Data show the size and nature of problems, so they help in making policy.

questions.q: Case: A government doubles a scheme’s budget after data show rising unemployment in 15–29 age group in three states. Which function of statistics?
questions.why: The government used data on unemployment to decide to raise the budget, so this is policy formulation using statistical data.

courses.title: Statistics Ch 2 · Collection of Data
courses.summary: Primary and secondary data and their sources in India, survey methods, good questionnaires and pilot surveys, census vs sample, random and non-random sampling, and sampling vs non-sampling errors.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish primary and secondary data and name Indian sources
Learners can design a good questionnaire
Learners can choose census or sample and a sampling method
Learners can identify sampling and non-sampling errors

story.title: Collect it yourself or borrow it?

scenes.text: Meena wants to study how much families in her colony spend on mobile data.
She can survey them herself — or use a government report.
Data come from primary or secondary sources.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Primary data**: collected *first-hand* by the investigator for a specific purpose (survey, interview, experiment). Original, suited to purpose, but costly and time-consuming.
- **Secondary data**: already collected by someone else and used by the investigator (Census reports, RBI bulletins, NSO surveys, Economic Survey, research papers). Cheap and quick, but must be checked for **suitability, adequacy and reliability**.

steps.title: Main secondary sources in India
steps.body:
- **Census of India** (Office of the Registrar General): population, literacy, households — normally every 10 years; the 2011 Census is the most recent completed one.
- **National Statistics Office (NSO)** under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI): national sample surveys (consumption, employment — e.g., Periodic Labour Force Survey), national accounts, Annual Survey of Industries.
- **RBI** publications, **Economic Survey** (Ministry of Finance), Labour Bureau, Directorate of Economics and Statistics (agriculture).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) Meena interviews 50 families → primary. (b) She uses PLFS unemployment rates → secondary. (c) A company uses its own sales records collected for another purpose → secondary for the new study.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Checks before using secondary data
steps.body: Ask: Who collected it and why? When? What definitions and units? Was it a sample or census? Is it reliable and adequate for my purpose?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking secondary data are always less accurate.
- Using secondary data with different definitions without adjusting.
- Forgetting that the same data are primary for the collector and secondary for others.

activity.prompt: Primary or secondary data for YOUR study?

quiz.why: Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for a particular purpose.

quiz.q: The Census of India is normally held every…
quiz.why: The Census of India is held once every 10 years, so it is decennial.
The National Statistical Office (NSO) is under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).
Before using secondary data, check whether they are suitable for your purpose, adequate and reliable.

quiz.q: A survey you conduct yourself gives…
quiz.why: A survey conducted by yourself gives first-hand information, so it is primary data.

lessons.title: Methods of collecting primary data and the questionnaire

scenes.text: Meena drafts a questionnaire: “Don’t you think data packs are too expensive?”
Her teacher says that is a leading question.
Good questionnaires are an art.

steps.title: Survey methods
steps.body:
- **Personal interviews**: face to face. Merits: high response, can clarify, observe. Limitations: costly, time-consuming, interviewer bias.
- **Mailing (or online) questionnaire**: sent by post/email/link. Merits: cheap, wide coverage, respondents answer privately. Limitations: low response rate, cannot clarify, only literate respondents.
- **Telephone interviews**: quick, cheap compared with personal, can clarify; but limited to phone users, short questions only, no observation.

steps.title: Qualities of a good questionnaire
steps.body:
- Short and simple; logical sequence (general → specific).
- Avoid **leading questions** (“Don’t you agree…?”), **ambiguous** words, **double-barrelled** questions (two questions in one), personal/sensitive questions early, calculations.
- Use **closed-ended** (multiple choice, yes/no) and **open-ended** questions wisely.
- Precise units and time references (“last 30 days”).

steps.title: Pilot survey
steps.body: A trial run of the questionnaire on a small group before the main survey to find unclear questions, estimate time and cost, and train interviewers.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Fix the question
steps.body: Bad: “Don’t you think data packs are too expensive and slow?” (leading + double-barrelled). Better: “How much did your household spend on mobile data in the last 30 days? (₹)” and separately “Rate your internet speed: Very slow / Slow / OK / Fast.”

steps.title: Solved example 2: Choose the method
steps.body: Survey of 2,000 college students across India quickly and cheaply → online questionnaire. Survey of elderly villagers with low literacy → personal interviews.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Asking questions that need calculations.
- Skipping the pilot survey.
- Using vague time periods (“recently”).

activity.prompt: Good question or bad question?

items.text: How many people live in your household?
Don’t you agree that our school is the best?
Do you like tea and coffee?
What was your monthly electricity bill last month (₹)?
What percentage of your income do you save after tax, rent and EMIs?

quiz.q: “Don’t you think smoking is bad?” is a…
