steps.body: Slow growth from the second half of the 19th century: **cotton textile mills** (mainly Indian-owned, in Maharashtra and Gujarat), **jute mills** (mainly foreign-owned, in Bengal). **Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO)** was incorporated in **1907**. After the Second World War some sugar, cement and paper industries grew. Capital goods industries were almost absent; public sector was limited to railways, power, communications, ports and some departmental undertakings.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Link the effects
steps.body: Cheap British cloth → handloom weavers lose work → move to farming → more pressure on land → lower farm incomes.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why no capital goods industry?
steps.body: Machines were imported from Britain; no policy encouraged machine tools → Indian industrial base stayed weak at independence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the jute industry was Indian-dominated (it was mainly foreign-owned).
- Giving TISCO’s year incorrectly — it was 1907.

activity.prompt: Match

quiz.why: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was incorporated in 1907.
Jute mills were mostly in Bengal, as jute was grown in that region.
Deindustrialisation is the decline of traditional handicraft industries, which could not compete with cheap machine-made British goods.

quiz.q: A reason for decline of handicrafts was…
quiz.why: Indian handicrafts declined because cheap machine-made British goods came in and the artisans could not compete.

quiz.q: Capital goods industries at independence were…
quiz.why: At independence India's capital goods industry, which makes machines, was almost absent, so the base for industry was weak.

lessons.title: Foreign trade and the drain of wealth

scenes.text: Ships left Bombay with raw cotton, jute and indigo.
They returned with British cloth and machinery.
India’s export surplus paid for British expenses.

steps.title: Pattern of trade
steps.body: India became an **exporter of primary products** (raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo, jute) and an **importer of finished consumer goods** (cotton, silk, woollen cloth) and capital goods from Britain. Britain had a **monopoly** over India’s trade; more than half went to Britain. The opening of the **Suez Canal (1869)** cut costs and time of shipping.

steps.title: Export surplus and drain
steps.body: India had a large **export surplus**, but it did not bring gold or goods to India. It was used to pay for British administrative expenses in India, war expenses, and imports of invisible items (shipping, banking, insurance) — the **“drain of wealth”** (Dadabhai Naoroji’s theory). This caused shortages of essential goods within India.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Why is an export surplus normally good, but not here?
steps.body: Normally an export surplus builds reserves for development. Under colonial rule, it financed Britain’s costs, so India’s people did not benefit.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Suez Canal effect
steps.body: Shorter route between Britain and India → cheaper transport → even more British control over Indian trade.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying India had a trade deficit — it had an export surplus.
- Thinking the surplus helped India’s development.

activity.prompt: Colonial India mainly exported or imported?

quiz.why: The Suez Canal opened in 1869. It shortened the sea route between Britain and India and made trade cheaper for Britain.

quiz.q: India’s colonial export surplus was used for…
quiz.why: India's export surplus was not used for Indian development. It paid for British administrative costs and wars, which is called the drain.

quiz.q: The “drain of wealth” theory is associated with…
quiz.why: Dadabhai Naoroji put forward the drain of wealth theory, arguing that wealth was flowing out of India to Britain.

quiz.q: More than half of India’s trade was with…
quiz.why: Britain had a monopoly on India's trade, and more than half of it was with Britain.
India exported mainly primary products, such as raw cotton, jute and indigo, and imported finished goods.

scenes.text: In 1947, many babies did not live to see their first birthday.
Life expectancy was about 32 years; literacy was below 20%.
Most workers were in agriculture.

steps.title: Demographic conditions
steps.body:
- The first census was in **1881**. Before **1921** population growth was slow; **1921** is called the **year of the great divide** (after it, population grew steadily: second stage of demographic transition).
- Both **birth and death rates were high**.
- **Overall literacy below 16%**; female literacy about 7%.
- **Infant mortality** about **218 per 1,000** live births (very high).
- **Life expectancy** about **32 years**.
- Poor public health facilities, frequent epidemics and famines; widespread poverty.

steps.title: Occupational structure
steps.body: About **70–75%** of the workforce in agriculture, **10%** in manufacturing and **15–20%** in services. Regional variation: some areas of Madras Presidency, Bombay and Bengal saw a fall in agriculture’s share, while Odisha, Rajasthan and Punjab saw a rise.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Interpret the data
steps.body: IMR 218 per 1,000 means about **one in five** babies died before age one. Today India’s IMR is far lower (in the 20s or below per 1,000) — a major improvement.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why so much dependence on agriculture?
steps.body: Deindustrialisation pushed artisans to farming, modern industry was small, and services were limited → agriculture absorbed most workers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 1921 the year India’s population started falling — it is when steady growth began.
- Confusing literacy (~16%) with life expectancy (~32 years).

activity.prompt: Match the indicator with its value around independence

quiz.q: The first census of India was in…
quiz.why: The first census of India was held in 1881, and then every ten years.
1921 is called the year of the great divide, because the population growth rate then started rising steadily after being irregular before.

quiz.q: Life expectancy at independence was about…
quiz.why: Life expectancy at independence was only about 32 years, which shows poor health care and living conditions.

quiz.q: Share of workforce in manufacturing was about…
quiz.why: Only about 10% of the workforce was in manufacturing, as industry was small. Most workers were in agriculture.
A high infant mortality rate (IMR) shows poor health conditions, such as poor sanitation and medical care.

lessons.title: Infrastructure and the state of the economy in 1947

scenes.text: In 1850 India’s first railway lines were built; by 1947 thousands of km had been laid.
They carried raw materials to ports and British goods inland.
Yet villages had few roads, schools or hospitals.

steps.title: Infrastructure under colonial rule
steps.body:
- **Railways** (introduced **1850**; first passenger train Bombay–Thane 1853): enabled long-distance travel, broke geographical and cultural barriers, and **commercialised agriculture**; but mainly served British trade and the social cost (famines’ spread of exports) was high; export of goods also displaced self-sufficiency.
- **Roads**: built mainly for army movement and to carry raw materials to ports; rural roads were scarce.
- **Ports, inland waterways**, **posts and telegraphs** (the latter mainly for law and order).
- **Shipping**: dominated by British companies.

steps.title: India at independence
steps.body: Stagnant agriculture, weak industry, export of raw materials, high poverty and unemployment, poor health and literacy, limited infrastructure. These conditions shaped the **planning priorities** after 1947: growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Positive and negative effects of railways
steps.body: Positive: travel, trade, unity, famine relief movement. Negative: served British interests, carried raw materials out, competed with local handicrafts by bringing cheap goods, inland waterways became uneconomical.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Connect to planning
steps.body: Because capital goods industry was absent, the Second Five Year Plan (1956) emphasised heavy industry through the public sector.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying railways were built mainly for Indians’ welfare.
- Mixing 1850 (railways introduced) and 1853 (first passenger train).

activity.prompt: Arrange the events

quiz.q: Railways in India were introduced in…
quiz.why: Railways were introduced in India in 1850, and the first line ran in 1853.

quiz.q: Roads in colonial India were built mainly…
quiz.why: Colonial roads were built mainly to move the army and to carry raw materials to ports. They did not serve villages.
Posts and telegraphs mainly served the colonial administration, helping maintain law and order.

quiz.q: A positive effect of railways was…
quiz.why: A positive effect of railways was breaking geographical barriers and linking regions, even though the colonial aim was British gain.

quiz.q: Shipping during colonial rule was dominated by…
quiz.why: Shipping during colonial rule was dominated by British companies, which also earned the freight income.

questions.q: Colonial policy made India a supplier of…
questions.why: Colonial policy made India a supplier of raw materials to Britain's industries and a market for its finished goods.

questions.q: TISCO was incorporated in…
questions.why: TISCO was incorporated in 1907, which was an early steel venture in India.

questions.q: Life expectancy at independence was about…
questions.why: Life expectancy in India at independence was about 32 years.

questions.q: Railways were introduced in…
questions.why: Railways were introduced in India in 1850. The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and the first census was in 1881.

questions.q: Zamindari system was associated with…
questions.why: The zamindari system, in which zamindars collected rent from cultivators, is linked with the Permanent Settlement of 1793.

questions.q: Year of the great divide:
questions.why: 1921 is called the year of the great divide, because India's population growth began to rise steadily after that.

questions.q: Assertion (A): India had an export surplus under colonial rule. Reason (R): The surplus was used to build Indian industries.
questions.why: The assertion is true, as India had an export surplus. The reason is false, because the surplus paid British administrative and war costs, not Indian industry.

questions.q: Jute industry was mainly…
questions.why: The jute industry was concentrated in Bengal and was mostly owned by foreigners.

questions.q: IMR around 1947:
questions.why: The infant mortality rate around 1947 was very high, about 218 per 1,000 live births.

questions.q: Case: A village’s weavers lose work after cheap British cloth arrives and start farming. This illustrates…
questions.why: Weavers who lose work because of cheap British cloth and turn to farming show deindustrialisation, with more pressure on land.

questions.q: Commercialisation of agriculture led to…
options: shift to cash crops for British industry
questions.why: Commercialisation of agriculture made farmers shift to cash crops, such as cotton and jute, for British industry rather than food crops.

questions.q: Case: About 72% of workers in agriculture, 10% in industry, 18% in services. Which period?
questions.why: About 72% of workers in agriculture, 10% in industry and 18% in services is the colonial structure of India at independence.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Indian agriculture was stagnant under British rule. Reason (R): Land settlement systems gave zamindars little incentive to invest.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Zamindars collected rent but had little reason to invest in land improvement, so agriculture stagnated.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
options: Capital goods industry was strong in 1947
questions.why: The false statement is that the capital goods industry was strong in 1947. It was almost absent. The other statements are true.

questions.q: Case: An economist argues India’s export surplus financed British war and administrative costs. This is the…
questions.why: The argument that India's export surplus paid British war and administrative costs is the drain of wealth theory, put forward by Naoroji.

questions.q: Case: Railways helped commercialise agriculture but also carried raw materials out and cheap goods in, hurting artisans. The best summary is…
options: railways had mixed effects that served colonial interests
questions.why: Railways helped commercialisation and link regions, but also carried raw materials out and cheap British goods in, hurting artisans. So the effects were mixed, serving colonial interests.

courses.title: IED Ch 2 · Indian Economy 1950–1990
courses.summary: Mixed economy and planning, goals of five-year plans, land reforms, the Green Revolution and subsidies, the public sector and IPR 1956, small-scale industry, import substitution and an appraisal of 1950–1990.
outcomes: Learners can explain the goals of planning and their conflicts
Learners can evaluate land reforms and the Green Revolution
Learners can describe IPR 1956, licensing and SSI policy
Learners can assess import substitution and the period as a whole

lessons.title: Planning and the goals of five-year plans

story.title: Drawing a roadmap for a new nation

scenes.text: In 1950, newly independent India had poverty, low literacy and a weak industrial base.
The government set up the Planning Commission with the Prime Minister as chairperson.
Plans for five years at a time set goals and priorities.

steps.title: Economic system and planning
steps.body:
India chose a **mixed economy** (both public and private sectors, with the state playing a leading role), inspired partly by socialist ideas but keeping democracy and private property. The **Planning Commission** was set up in **1950**; the **First Five Year Plan** began in **1951**. The Planning Commission was replaced by **NITI Aayog** on **1 January 2015**.

**P.C. Mahalanobis** is regarded as the architect of the **Second Plan (1956–61)**, which emphasised heavy industry.

steps.title: Goals of five-year plans
steps.body:
- **Growth**: increase in GDP — the country’s capacity to produce goods and services (capital, technology, efficiency).
- **Modernisation**: adopting new technology and also social changes (e.g., women’s rights).
- **Self-reliance**: reduce dependence on foreign countries, especially for food and capital goods.
- **Equity**: benefits of growth should reach the poor; reduce inequality.

Goals can conflict (e.g., modern machines raise output but may reduce jobs), so plans balance them.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the goal
steps.body: (a) Building more steel plants → growth and self-reliance. (b) Using tractors and HYV seeds → modernisation. (c) Land redistribution to landless → equity.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Conflict of goals
steps.body: Introducing labour-saving machines raises output (growth, modernisation) but may increase unemployment (against equity) → the plan must add job programmes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying India adopted a pure socialist economy.
- Saying the Planning Commission still exists (replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015).
- Confusing GDP growth with equity.

activity.prompt: Match the term
pairs: Set up in 1950, chaired by the PM

quiz.q: Planning Commission was set up in…
quiz.why: The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950. The first Five Year Plan began in 1951.

quiz.q: First Five Year Plan began in…
quiz.why: The First Five Year Plan began in 1951 and ran to 1956.

quiz.q: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in…
quiz.why: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.

quiz.q: Increase in GDP relates to the goal of…
quiz.why: An increase in GDP, which means more goods and services, is the planning goal of growth.
India adopted a mixed economy, with both public and private sectors working together.

scenes.text: Ramu has tilled the same land for decades but owns none of it.
Land reforms after 1950 aimed to give tillers ownership.
Results were mixed across states.

steps.title: Why land reforms?
steps.body: At independence, land was very unequally distributed; tillers had little incentive because intermediaries took most of the surplus. **Land to the tiller** policy aimed at equity and higher productivity (owners invest more).

steps.title: Main measures
steps.body:
- **Abolition of intermediaries** (zamindars): tillers became owners; about 200 lakh tenants came into direct contact with the government.
- **Land ceiling**: fixing the maximum land an individual can own; surplus redistributed to landless.
- **Tenancy reforms**: regulating rent, security of tenure.

**Successes**: Kerala and West Bengal (governments committed to land-to-tiller). **Limitations**: in many states, landlords used loopholes (transferring land to relatives), ceiling laws were poorly implemented, and some former zamindars kept large holdings by claiming self-cultivation.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Why did ownership raise output?
steps.body: A tenant who becomes owner keeps the gain from investment (well, better seeds) → invests more → productivity rises.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why did ceiling fail in many places?
steps.body: Big landholders challenged laws in courts and registered land in relatives’ names (benami) → little surplus land actually redistributed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying land reforms succeeded uniformly across India.
- Confusing land ceiling (maximum limit) with land consolidation.

statements.s: Land ceiling fixes the maximum land a person can own.
Land reforms were equally successful in all states.
statements.why: Kerala and West Bengal did better.

statements.s: Abolition of intermediaries brought tenants into direct contact with government.
Landlords never used loopholes.

quiz.why: 'Land to the tiller' means that ownership of the land goes to those who actually cultivate it.

quiz.q: States with relatively successful land reforms:
quiz.why: Land reforms were relatively successful in Kerala and West Bengal, where state governments were committed to them.
A land ceiling limits how much land one person can own, so it reduces concentration of land ownership and promotes equity.
Land ceilings often failed because landlords used loopholes and transferred land to others in false (benami) names.
When cultivators own the land, they have a reason to invest in improving it, since they keep the gains.

lessons.title: The Green Revolution and the subsidy debate

scenes.text: In the early 1960s India depended on food imports.
High-yielding varieties (HYV) of wheat and rice transformed Punjab’s fields.
By the 1970s India was self-sufficient in food grains.

steps.title: What the Green Revolution was
steps.body:
A large increase in food grain production from the **mid-1960s** using **HYV seeds** together with adequate **fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation**. First phase (mid-1960s to mid-1970s): mainly **wheat**, in Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu; second phase (mid-1970s to mid-1980s): spread to more states and crops.

**Marketed surplus**: portion of output sold in the market. Higher marketed surplus lowered food prices relative to other goods and allowed government to build **buffer stocks**.

steps.title: Risks and responses
steps.body:
- Small farmers might not afford inputs → government gave **loans at low interest** and **subsidies** on fertilisers.
- Pest attacks risk → research institutes provided services.
- Benefits were concentrated in some regions and among richer farmers initially.

steps.title: The subsidy debate
steps.body: **For**: encourage new technology, help small farmers, keep food affordable. **Against**: benefits often go to fertiliser industry and richer farmers, burden on government finances, overuse of fertiliser and water harms soil and groundwater. View: subsidies should be targeted and reformed, not abolished abruptly.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Marketed surplus
steps.body: A farmer produces 100 quintals of wheat, keeps 30 for family and seed → marketed surplus = **70 quintals**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why did prices fall?
steps.body: More marketed surplus from many farmers → supply rose faster than demand → relative food prices fell, helping poor consumers who spend a large share of income on food.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Green Revolution began with rice in eastern India — the first phase was mainly wheat in Punjab and a few states.
- Saying HYV seeds work without irrigation and fertilisers.

activity.prompt: A farmer harvests 80 quintals of rice and keeps 25 quintals for home use and seed. What is the marketed surplus (quintals)?

quiz.why: HYV (high yielding variety) seeds give high output only with a package of assured irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides.

quiz.q: The first phase of the Green Revolution mainly covered…
quiz.why: In the first phase of the Green Revolution, HYV seeds were used mainly for wheat in Punjab, Haryana and western UP.
Marketed surplus is the part of output that the farmer sells in the market, after keeping some for own use.

options: burden on government and overuse of inputs
quiz.why: An argument against subsidies is that they burden the government's budget and encourage overuse of inputs such as fertiliser.
The Green Revolution started in the mid-1960s with HYV seeds.

lessons.title: Industry: public sector, IPR 1956 and small-scale industry

scenes.text: In the 1950s private industrialists lacked capital to build steel plants.
The government built them — Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur.
Private firms needed a licence to start or expand.

steps.title: Public and private sectors in industrial development
steps.body: Indian industrialists lacked capital and the market was small, so the **state took the lead** in heavy and basic industries. The goal was a socialist pattern of society with the state controlling the “commanding heights” of the economy.

steps.title: Industrial Policy Resolution 1956
steps.body:
Classified industries into three categories:
1. Industries **exclusively owned by the state**.
2. Industries where the **private sector could supplement** state-owned enterprises (state would start new units).
3. Remaining industries left to the **private sector**.

Private sector was controlled by **industrial licensing** — a licence was needed to start a new firm or expand output. Licensing was used to promote industries in **backward regions** and to prevent over-production; concessions (tax benefits, cheap power) were given in backward areas.

steps.title: Small-scale industry (SSI)
steps.body: Karve Committee (1955) noted the potential of village and small industries for employment. SSI was defined by maximum investment in assets (limits revised over time). Policy measures: **reservation** of many products for SSI, concessions such as lower excise duty and cheaper loans. Rationale: labour-intensive, more employment, regional spread.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify under IPR 1956
steps.body: Atomic energy and railways → category 1 (state exclusive). Machine tools, fertilisers → category 2 (state plus private). Consumer goods like soap → category 3 (private).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Licensing outcome
steps.body: A firm wanting to expand textile output had to get a licence; the government could refuse if capacity seemed enough, or approve in a backward district with concessions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying private sector was banned — it was regulated.
- Confusing IPR 1956 with the 1991 New Industrial Policy.

activity.prompt: IPR 1956 category

quiz.why: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 classified industries into three categories: those exclusive to the state, those open to both, and those left to the private sector.

options: promote backward regions and control capacity
quiz.why: Industrial licensing was used to control capacity and to promote industries in backward regions.
The Karve Committee (1955) looked at the development of village and small-scale industries.

quiz.q: Reason the state took the lead in heavy industry:
options: private sector had too much capital
quiz.why: The state took the lead in heavy industry because the private sector lacked the large capital needed.

quiz.q: Reservation of products for SSI aimed at…
options: employment and protection of small units
quiz.why: Reserving products for small-scale industries aimed at protecting them from big firms, and so it supported employment.

lessons.title: Trade policy: import substitution and an appraisal of 1950–1990

story.title: Make it here, don’t import it

scenes.text: In the 1960s an Indian family could rarely buy a foreign car or TV.
High tariffs and quotas kept imports out to protect domestic industry.
Protection helped industry grow — but also made it inefficient.

steps.title: Import substitution (inward-looking trade)
steps.body:
Replace imports with domestic production. Tools: **tariffs** (taxes on imports, making them expensive) and **quotas** (limits on quantity imported). Rationale: protect **infant industries** from foreign competition until they mature; save foreign exchange.

Effects: the share of industry in GDP rose (about 11.8% in 1950–51 to about 24.6% in 1990–91); industry diversified; India came to produce a wide range of goods. But many firms became inefficient due to lack of competition; consumer choice was limited; exports suffered.

steps.title: Criticisms of 1950–1990 policies
steps.body:
- **Public sector inefficiency**: many PSUs made losses but continued (some were in areas where state control was not essential).
- **Licence–permit Raj**: licences used to prevent competition, delays and corruption.
- **Protection** removed incentive to improve quality.
- **Inward-looking trade** limited export growth.

Achievements: self-sufficiency in food grains, diversified industrial base, growth of infrastructure, equity measures (land reforms).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Tariff effect
steps.body: Imported radio ₹1,000 + 100% tariff = ₹2,000; domestic radio ₹1,500 → consumers buy the domestic one even if quality is lower → industry protected.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Quota effect
steps.body: Government allows only 10,000 imported cars a year → limited supply → high prices for imports; domestic makers face little competition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying protection had no benefits — it helped build a diverse industrial base.
- Confusing tariff (tax) with quota (quantity limit).

activity.prompt: Match
pairs: Produce at home instead of importing

quiz.why: A tariff is a tax on imported goods, which makes them costlier.
Import substitution means making at home the goods that were imported, so as to reduce dependence on imports.

quiz.q: Industry’s share of GDP in 1990–91 was about…
quiz.why: Industry's share of GDP rose from 11.8% in 1950–51 to about 24.6% in 1990–91.
A criticism of the 1950–90 policy is that protected industries, shielded from competition, became inefficient.
A quota limits the quantity of goods that can be imported, whereas a tariff taxes them.

questions.q: Planning Commission was set up in…
questions.why: The Planning Commission was set up in 1950.

questions.q: Architect of the Second Five Year Plan:
questions.why: P.C. Mahalanobis was the architect of the Second Five Year Plan, which stressed heavy industry.

questions.q: Goals of planning include…
questions.why: The goals of Indian planning were growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity.

questions.q: HYV seeds are associated with…
questions.why: HYV seeds are associated with the Green Revolution of the mid-1960s.

questions.q: A tariff is a…
questions.why: A tariff is a tax on imports.

questions.q: Land ceiling means…
questions.why: A land ceiling sets a maximum limit on how much land a person can own.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Marketed surplus increased after the Green Revolution. Reason (R): HYV seeds raised output per hectare.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. HYV seeds raised output per hectare, so farmers had more to sell, and marketed surplus rose.

questions.q: IPR 1956: atomic energy falls in…
questions.why: Under the IPR 1956, industries such as atomic energy were in the first category, reserved exclusively for the state.

questions.q: Case: A farmer produces 120 quintals and keeps 40. Marketed surplus?
questions.why: Marketed surplus = total output − the amount kept = 120 − 40 = 80 quintals.

questions.q: Case: Domestic TV ₹20,000; imported TV ₹15,000 + 50% tariff. Consumer cost of imported TV?
questions.why: A 50% tariff raises the price by half: ₹15,000 × 1.5 = ₹22,500.

questions.q: Which states were relatively successful in land reforms?
questions.why: Kerala and West Bengal were relatively successful in land reforms, as their governments were committed to them.

questions.q: Case: A new car company is protected from imports for 15 years and becomes inefficient. Criticism?
questions.why: A firm that is protected from import competition for years has little reason to improve. This is a criticism of protection, as it causes inefficiency.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Fertiliser subsidies may harm the environment. Reason (R): Cheap fertiliser encourages overuse.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Cheap fertiliser encourages overuse, which can harm soil and water.

questions.q: Which pair conflicts most directly?
questions.why: Modernisation, which often uses labour-saving machines, conflicts most directly with employment and equity, since it may reduce jobs.

questions.q: NITI Aayog came into existence on…
questions.why: NITI Aayog came into existence on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission.

questions.q: Case: Government allows only 5,000 imported phones per year. Policy tool?
questions.why: A fixed limit on the number of imported phones is a quota, which restricts the quantity.

questions.q: Case: Industry share rose from 11.8% to 24.6% of GDP but many PSUs ran losses. A balanced appraisal is…
options: planning built an industrial base but with inefficiencies
questions.why: Industry's share rose strongly, so planning built an industrial base, but many PSUs ran losses. So the balanced view is that it built an industrial base with inefficiencies.

courses.title: IED Ch 3 · Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
courses.summary: The 1991 crisis, stabilisation and structural reforms, liberalisation of industry, finance, tax, foreign exchange and trade, privatisation and disinvestment, globalisation, outsourcing, the WTO, and a balanced assessment of reforms.
outcomes: Learners can explain the background of the 1991 reforms
Learners can describe liberalisation measures sector by sector
Learners can explain privatisation, disinvestment and globalisation
Learners can give a balanced appraisal of the reforms

lessons.title: The 1991 crisis and the need for reforms

scenes.text: In 1990–91, oil prices spiked during the Gulf war.
India’s foreign exchange reserves fell to an amount that could pay for only about two weeks of imports.
India turned to the IMF and World Bank — and launched sweeping reforms.

steps.title: Background of the crisis
steps.body:
- **Fiscal crisis**: government spending far exceeded revenue (large fiscal deficit); borrowing rose; interest burden grew.
- **Balance of payments crisis**: imports (especially oil) far exceeded exports; foreign borrowing rose; reserves fell sharply.
- Rising prices (inflation) and the Gulf war added to stress.
- India borrowed about $7 billion from the **IBRD (World Bank)** and the **IMF**, which expected reforms.

steps.title: The New Economic Policy (1991)
steps.body:
Announced in July 1991. Two groups of measures:
- **Stabilisation measures** (short-term): correct BoP and inflation — maintain reserves, control rising prices.
- **Structural reform measures** (long-term): improve efficiency and international competitiveness by removing rigidities.

The policy is summarised as **Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation (LPG)**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify the measure
steps.body: Devaluation of the rupee to boost exports quickly → stabilisation. Abolishing industrial licensing → structural reform.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why reserves matter
steps.body: Reserves of $1 billion with monthly imports of $2 billion cover only about 2 weeks → creditors stop lending → crisis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the reforms began in 1985 entirely — some liberalisation happened in the 1980s, but the major package came in 1991.
- Confusing stabilisation (short-term) with structural (long-term) measures.

activity.prompt: Stabilisation or structural reform?

items.text: Open sectors to private and foreign investment

options: balance of payments and fiscal crisis
quiz.why: The 1991 crisis was a balance of payments crisis, with very low forex reserves, along with a fiscal crisis.
India borrowed from the IMF and the World Bank in 1991, which asked for reforms in return.
Structural reforms aim at long-term efficiency and competitiveness. Stabilisation measures are short-term.
LPG stands for Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation.
A fiscal deficit means government spending is more than its revenue, so it must borrow.

lessons.title: Liberalisation: industry, finance, tax, foreign exchange and trade

scenes.text: In the 1980s, a car maker needed government licences to expand.
After 1991, most licences were abolished.
Liberalisation removed many controls across sectors.

steps.title: Industrial sector
steps.body:
- **Industrial licensing abolished** for almost all products except a short list — today mainly alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronic aerospace and defence equipment, and drugs and pharmaceuticals (some items vary over time).
- Industries reserved for the public sector cut to a few (now mainly **atomic energy** and **railway operations**).
- Many products de-reserved from small-scale industry; market forces to decide prices in many cases.

steps.title: Financial sector
steps.body: RBI shifted from **regulator to facilitator** of the financial sector. Private (Indian and foreign) banks allowed; foreign investment limits in banks raised; banks given freedom to open branches (with conditions); **Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs)** like merchant bankers, mutual funds and pension funds allowed to invest in Indian markets. SEBI given statutory powers (1992).

steps.title: Tax, foreign exchange and trade
steps.body:
- **Tax reforms**: reduction in income-tax and corporate tax rates; simplified procedures; **GST** introduced in 2017 to unify indirect taxes.
- **Foreign exchange**: rupee **devalued** in 1991; later the exchange rate became largely **market-determined**.
- **Trade and investment**: import licensing dismantled (except hazardous/environment-sensitive goods), quantitative restrictions on imports removed (fully by April 2001), tariffs reduced, export duties removed.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the reform
steps.body: (a) A foreign bank opens branches in Mumbai → financial sector. (b) Peak customs duty falls → trade policy. (c) A firm expands car output without licence → industrial deregulation.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Devaluation effect
steps.body: If $1 = ₹20 becomes $1 = ₹25, an Indian shirt priced ₹500 falls from $25 to $20 for foreign buyers → exports become cheaper → exports rise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying licensing was abolished for every industry.
- Saying RBI stopped regulating banks — it became a facilitator while still regulating.
- Confusing devaluation with depreciation (devaluation is a deliberate official cut under fixed rates).

activity.prompt: Match the reform to the sector
pairs: Entry of private and foreign banks

options: a facilitator rather than only a regulator
quiz.why: After 1991 the RBI's role changed from regulator to facilitator, as financial sector decisions were freed to the market.

quiz.q: Industries still reserved for the public sector today mainly include…
quiz.why: Only a very few industries remain reserved for the public sector today, mainly atomic energy and railway operations.
Devaluation lowers the foreign currency price of a country's goods, so exports become cheaper abroad.
Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) include mutual funds, pension funds and similar institutions.

quiz.q: Quantitative restrictions on imports were fully removed by…
quiz.why: Quantitative restrictions (quotas) on imports were fully removed by April 2001.

scenes.text: The government owned 100% of many companies.
Some were inefficient; the government also needed money.
It began selling part of its shares — disinvestment.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body:
**Privatisation** means shedding of ownership or management of a government-owned enterprise: (a) transferring ownership/management to the private sector, or (b) outright sale; or (c) **disinvestment** — selling part of government equity in PSUs to the public/private investors.

Aims: improve financial discipline and efficiency, raise resources, encourage modernisation, let markets judge performance.

steps.title: Navratna and related policies
steps.body: To improve efficiency and autonomy, profitable PSUs were given special status: **Maharatna**, **Navratna** and **Miniratna**, with greater freedom in investment and operations. (Navratna status began in 1997; Maharatna was added later.) Examples have included IOCL and ONGC (Maharatna), and others in Navratna/Miniratna lists that change over time.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Disinvestment math
steps.body: Government owns 90% of a PSU with 100 crore shares. It sells 10% of total shares (10 crore shares) at ₹200 each → raises **₹2,000 crore**; its holding falls to **80%** (still majority).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Effect on efficiency
steps.body: After partial listing, the PSU must publish results to shareholders and face market scrutiny → pressure to improve efficiency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying disinvestment always means full privatisation — often it is partial.
- Saying Navratna PSUs are private companies — they remain public sector.

activity.prompt: Government holds 75% of a PSU with 200 crore shares. It sells 25 crore shares. What is its new holding (%)?

options: selling part of government equity in PSUs
quiz.why: Disinvestment means the government sells part of its shareholding in public sector undertakings.
Navratna status gives a profitable PSU more autonomy, such as freedom to invest without prior approval.
One aim of privatisation is to bring better financial discipline and efficiency.

quiz.q: After selling 10% from a 90% holding, the government owns…
quiz.why: If the government sells 10 percentage points of a 90% holding, it is left with 90 − 10 = 80%, which is still a majority.
Navratna companies are public sector enterprises given extra autonomy.

story.title: Your call is answered in Pune

scenes.text: A customer in Texas calls a helpline; the answer comes from Pune.
Indian firms now sell software, medicines and cars worldwide.
Globalisation and WTO rules shaped this.

steps.title: Globalisation
steps.body:
Integration of the national economy with the world economy through trade, investment, technology, people and ideas. It results from liberalisation of trade and investment policies.

- **Outsourcing**: firms hire outside (often foreign) agencies for services such as call centres, data processing, accounting, medical transcription, banking services, music recording, film editing, teaching. India is a leading destination because of skilled, English-speaking workers at lower cost and good communication technology.

steps.title: World Trade Organization (WTO)
steps.body: Founded in **1995** as successor to **GATT** (1948). Aims: a rule-based trade regime; remove tariff and non-tariff barriers; open markets for goods **and services**; protect intellectual property (TRIPS); dispute settlement. India has been a member since the beginning and has reduced tariffs and removed quotas; it also argues for developing countries’ interests (agriculture subsidies of rich countries, etc.).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify globalisation
steps.body: (a) An Indian pharma firm sells generics in Africa → trade integration. (b) A US bank sets up a back office in Hyderabad → outsourcing/FDI. (c) Foreign funds buy Indian shares → financial integration.

steps.title: Solved example 2: WTO concern
steps.body: Developed countries subsidise their farmers heavily; developing countries say this makes their farm exports uncompetitive → a long-running WTO debate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying WTO was created in 1948 (that was GATT).
- Thinking globalisation only means imports.

statements.s: WTO succeeded GATT in 1995.
Outsourcing includes call centres and medical transcription.
WTO deals only with goods, not services.
India joined the WTO only in 2010.

quiz.why: The World Trade Organization (WTO) was established in 1995, replacing GATT.

options: skilled English-speaking workers at lower cost
quiz.why: India attracts outsourcing because it has skilled, English-speaking workers who cost less than in developed countries.
Globalisation is the integration of an economy with the world economy, through trade, investment and technology.
TRIPS is the WTO agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights.
The WTO replaced GATT, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, in 1995.

lessons.title: Indian economy during reforms: an assessment

scenes.text: GDP growth rose; India became a big services exporter.
But farmers faced distress and many jobs stayed informal.
Economists debate the results.

steps.title: Positive outcomes
steps.body:
- Higher GDP growth (driven largely by services; industry growth was uneven).
- Rise in **FDI and FII** inflows; large **foreign exchange reserves** (India among the largest holders).
- Growth of exports of software, auto parts, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals.
- More consumer choice and competition; telecom and IT revolution.

steps.title: Criticisms
steps.body:
- **Growth and employment**: growth did not create enough good-quality jobs (“jobless growth” concern).
- **Agriculture neglected**: public investment in agriculture (irrigation, power, roads, research) fell; removal of fertiliser subsidies raised costs; export-oriented shift to cash crops reduced food crops in some areas.
- **Industry**: cheaper imports hurt some domestic industries; infrastructure gaps; developed countries’ non-tariff barriers.
- **Disinvestment**: assets sometimes undervalued; proceeds used to cover deficits rather than build assets.
- **Fiscal policies**: tax cuts reduced revenue in the short run; tax incentives for foreign investment limited the scope for public spending.

steps.title: Demonetisation and GST (later reforms)
steps.body: In **November 2016**, ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes were withdrawn (demonetisation) to target black money, counterfeit notes and promote digital payments; its effects remain debated. **GST** (July 2017) unified indirect taxes into one system.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Evaluate a statement
steps.body: “Reforms benefited all sectors equally.” → Not accurate: services grew fastest; agriculture faced distress; growth was uneven across regions and groups.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Case
steps.body: A small toy maker closes after cheap imports enter; at the same time an IT firm hires 5,000 engineers → reforms create winners and losers; policy must support those who lose out.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing only positives or only negatives — exam answers need a balanced view.
- Stating exact growth figures you are unsure of; use trends.

activity.prompt: Outcome of reforms: positive or a criticism?

items.text: Fall in public investment in agriculture
Undervaluation of PSU assets in disinvestment

quiz.q: Post-reform growth was led mainly by…
quiz.why: Post-reform growth in India was led mainly by the services sector.

quiz.q: A criticism of reforms in agriculture:
quiz.why: A criticism of reforms in agriculture is the fall in public investment, such as in irrigation and rural infrastructure.

quiz.q: Demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes was in…
quiz.why: Demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes took place in November 2016.
Jobless growth means the economy grows, but without enough new jobs being created.
A balanced assessment lists both the benefits and the criticisms of reforms, with examples.

questions.q: The NEP of 1991 was triggered by…
questions.why: The New Economic Policy of 1991 was triggered by a balance of payments and fiscal crisis.

questions.q: LPG: “P” stands for…
questions.why: In LPG, P stands for Privatisation, the shift of ownership or management from the public to the private sector.

questions.q: WTO was set up in…
questions.why: The WTO was set up in 1995.

questions.q: Disinvestment means…
questions.why: Disinvestment is the sale of the government's shares (equity) in public sector undertakings.

questions.q: Stabilisation measures are…
questions.why: Stabilisation measures are short-term steps to correct problems like the balance of payments and inflation. Structural reforms are long-term.

questions.q: After 1991, RBI changed from…
questions.why: After 1991 the RBI moved from being only a regulator of the financial sector to also being a facilitator.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Devaluation of rupee in 1991 aimed to boost exports. Reason (R): Devaluation makes Indian goods cheaper in foreign currency.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Devaluation makes Indian goods cheaper in foreign currency, so it helps boost exports.

questions.q: Which is a structural reform?
questions.why: Abolishing industrial licensing is a structural reform, since it changes the economy's rules for the long term.

questions.q: Case: $1 = ₹40 becomes $1 = ₹50. A ₹2,000 product costs a US buyer…
questions.why: At ₹40 per dollar, ₹2,000 costs $50. At ₹50 per dollar, it costs $40. The rupee has become weaker, so the product is cheaper for the US buyer.

questions.q: Case: Govt owns 85% of a PSU and sells 15% of total shares. New holding?
questions.why: The government sells 15 percentage points of the shares, so its holding is 85% − 15% = 70%.

questions.q: Which is a criticism of reforms?
questions.why: A criticism of reforms is the reduced public investment in agriculture. The others are positive results.

questions.q: Case: A US hospital sends patient records to be transcribed in Chennai. This is…
questions.why: Hiring a firm abroad to do work such as transcription is outsourcing.

questions.q: Assertion (A): WTO deals only with trade in goods. Reason (R): WTO succeeded GATT.
questions.why: The assertion is false, since the WTO also covers services and intellectual property, not only goods. The reason is true, as the WTO succeeded GATT.

questions.q: Navratna status is given to…
questions.why: Navratna status is given to profitable PSUs, to give them greater autonomy in decisions.

questions.q: Case: Reserves of $2 billion; monthly imports $4 billion. Import cover?
questions.why: Import cover = reserves ÷ monthly imports = 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5 month, which is about 2 weeks.

questions.q: Case: GDP grows 7% but formal employment barely rises and farm incomes stagnate. Which criticism fits?
questions.why: Growth of 7% with little rise in jobs is jobless growth, and stagnant farm incomes point to neglect of agriculture. Both are criticisms of reforms.

questions.q: Which industries remain reserved for the public sector mainly?
questions.why: Only a few industries, mainly atomic energy and railway operations, remain reserved for the public sector.

courses.title: IED Ch 4 · Human Capital Formation in India
courses.summary: Meaning and sources of human capital, its link with growth, human capital vs human development, education in India (RTE, NEP 2020, spending) and health as human capital.
outcomes: Learners can list and explain sources of human capital
Learners can distinguish human capital from human development
Learners can describe India’s education policies and spending gap
Learners can explain the role of health in human capital

lessons.title: Meaning and sources of human capital

scenes.text: Priya’s parents spend on her engineering degree; the village builds a health centre.
Ten years later, Priya earns well and pays taxes; healthy workers produce more.
Spending on people is an investment — human capital.

steps.title: Physical and human capital
steps.body: **Physical capital**: machines, buildings, tools. **Human capital**: the stock of skill, knowledge and health embodied in people (engineers, doctors, teachers, skilled workers). Converting people into a productive resource is **human capital formation**.

steps.title: Sources of human capital formation
steps.body:
- **Expenditure on education**: most important; raises earning capacity.
- **Expenditure on health**: preventive (vaccination), curative (treatment), social medicine (health literacy), clean water and sanitation.
- **On-the-job training**: firms train workers (in-house or outside).
- **Migration**: people move for better jobs; cost of migration is investment.
- **Expenditure on information**: about job markets, education, health — helps better decisions.

steps.title: Physical vs human capital
steps.body: Physical capital is tangible, can be sold, separable from owner, depreciates with use. Human capital is intangible, cannot be sold (only services), inseparable from its owner, depreciates with age but can be renewed by learning; it also creates social benefits (educated citizens, healthier communities).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the source
steps.body: (a) A company teaches its staff new software → on-the-job training. (b) A family spends on vaccination → health. (c) A worker moves from Bihar to Bengaluru for a better job → migration. (d) A student visits a career portal → information.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Return on education
steps.body: Cost of a 4-year diploma ₹2 lakh; it raises annual income by ₹60,000. Payback in about **3.3 years** of work; afterwards it keeps paying for decades — like investment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating education spending only as consumption.
- Forgetting migration and information as sources.
- Saying human capital can be sold like a machine.

activity.prompt: Which source of human capital?

items.text: Moving to a city for work

options: skills, knowledge and health of people
quiz.why: Human capital means the skills, knowledge and health of people, which make them more productive.

quiz.q: Most important source of human capital:
quiz.why: Education is the most important source of human capital formation, since it builds skills and knowledge.
Human capital is inseparable from its owner, since skills and knowledge are in the person and cannot be sold apart from them.
Vaccination prevents disease before it occurs, so it is preventive health care.
On-the-job training is provided by firms to their workers, to improve their skills while they work.

lessons.title: Human capital, economic growth and human development

scenes.text: Two factories have the same machines; one has trained workers.
The trained team produces 30% more and makes fewer mistakes.
Growth and human capital feed each other.

steps.title: Human capital and growth
steps.body:
- Educated and healthy workers are more **productive**.
- Human capital stimulates **innovation** and the ability to absorb new technology.
- Growth raises incomes, enabling more spending on education and health → two-way causality.
- Evidence: both human capital and GDP have risen in India over time, though measurement of the causal link is difficult.
- India’s IT success is often linked to its pool of skilled, English-speaking graduates.

steps.title: Human capital vs human development
steps.body: **Human capital** sees education and health as *means* to raise productivity. **Human development** sees them as *ends* in themselves — essential to well-being, whether or not they raise output (e.g., literacy and long life are valuable for their own sake). The UNDP’s Human Development Index combines life expectancy, education and income.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Means or end?
steps.body: A government says: “We fund education because it makes workers productive.” → human capital view. Another says: “Every child must read and write, because it enriches life.” → human development view.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Two-way link
steps.body: A state raises school spending → more skilled youth → firms invest → incomes rise → more tax revenue → more school spending.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating human capital and human development as identical.
- Claiming the causal link is precisely measured.

statements.s: Human development treats education as an end in itself.
Human capital and growth are unrelated.
HDI includes life expectancy, education and income.
Human capital views health as a means to productivity.

quiz.q: The human development view treats education and health as…
quiz.why: The human development view treats education and health as ends in themselves, as they improve people's lives directly, and not only as means to income.
The Human Development Index (HDI) is published by the UNDP.
Educated workers are more productive and innovative, which adds to economic growth.

quiz.q: Relationship between growth and human capital is…
quiz.why: Growth and human capital work both ways: more human capital helps growth, and growth gives resources for education and health.

quiz.q: India’s IT growth is often linked to…
quiz.why: India's IT growth is often linked to its pool of skilled human capital.

lessons.title: Education in India: growth, expenditure and policy

scenes.text: In 1951, India’s literacy rate was about 18%; by 2011 it was about 74%.
Laws and programmes pushed schooling for all.
But quality and spending remain challenges.

steps.title: Who invests and why government must
steps.body: Education and health are provided by both government and private sector. Government role is essential because individuals may under-invest (benefits spread to society), information gaps, and the poor cannot afford private services. Ministries of Education and Health at the Centre and States, with bodies like **NCERT**, **UGC** (universities), **AICTE** (technical education) and **ICMR** (medical research).

steps.title: Expenditure and key policies
steps.body:
- Public expenditure on education has generally been around **3–4.6% of GDP**, below the **6%** recommended by the **Kothari Commission (1964–66)** and reiterated by the National Education Policy 2020.
- **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009** (RTE): free and compulsory education for children aged **6–14**.
- Education cess (2% from 2004; now part of a 4% health and education cess on income tax).
- **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020**: 5+3+3+4 structure, foundational literacy and numeracy, multidisciplinary higher education.
- Programmes such as Samagra Shiksha and PM POSHAN (mid-day meals).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Literacy progress
steps.body: Literacy 1951 ≈ 18%; 2011 ≈ 74% → increase of about **56 percentage points** in 60 years. Female literacy (2011) ≈ 65% vs male ≈ 82% → gender gap remains.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Spending gap
steps.body: If GDP is ₹300 lakh crore, 6% = ₹18 lakh crore; at 4.5% = ₹13.5 lakh crore → gap of **₹4.5 lakh crore** a year.

steps.title: Challenges and prospects
steps.body: Quality of learning, teacher shortages, dropouts at secondary level, gender and regional gaps, rising private costs, need for vocational skills. Future: universal secondary education, skill programmes (e.g., Skill India), digital learning, higher research spending.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying RTE covers ages 3–18 (it covers 6–14).
- Quoting 6% of GDP as current spending — it is the *target*.

activity.prompt: If GDP is ₹200 lakh crore and education spending is 4%, by how much (₹ lakh crore) would spending have to rise to reach 6%?

quiz.why: The Right to Education Act (2009) covers children aged 6 to 14 years.

quiz.q: Kothari Commission recommended education spending of…
quiz.why: The Kothari Commission recommended spending 6% of GDP on education.
The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) regulates technical education.

quiz.q: NEP 2020 introduced a school structure of…
quiz.why: NEP 2020 replaced the 10+2 structure with a 5+3+3+4 structure for schooling.

quiz.q: Literacy in India in 2011 was about…
quiz.why: India's literacy rate was about 74% in the 2011 Census.

lessons.title: Health as human capital and the way forward

scenes.text: A worker with untreated malaria misses 20 days of work.
A vaccination and clean-water drive cuts illness in the village.
Health spending raises productivity and well-being.

steps.title: Why health matters
steps.body: Healthy people work more days, learn better and live longer, raising lifetime productivity. Health spending includes preventive medicine (vaccination), curative medicine (treatment), social medicine (health awareness), safe drinking water and sanitation.

steps.title: Bodies and programmes
steps.body: The **Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)** coordinates medical research. Programmes include universal immunisation, National Health Mission, and health insurance for poor households (e.g., Ayushman Bharat – PM-JAY). India’s public health spending has been low compared with many countries, leading to high out-of-pocket costs for families.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Productivity gain
steps.body: A workforce of 1,000 loses 10 days per worker per year to illness; a health programme halves this → **5,000 workdays** gained per year.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Social benefit
steps.body: Vaccinating children protects even unvaccinated neighbours by reducing spread → benefits to society exceed private benefits → reason for public provision.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting only hospitals as health spending (water and sanitation matter too).
- Ignoring out-of-pocket costs as a burden on poor households.

activity.prompt: 500 workers each lose 8 days a year to illness. A health drive cuts this by 75%. How many workdays are gained per year?

quiz.why: The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) coordinates and promotes medical research.

quiz.q: Safe drinking water is part of…
quiz.why: Providing safe drinking water prevents disease, so it is part of health spending, as preventive care.

options: families pay directly for health care
quiz.why: Out-of-pocket spending means households pay directly for health care from their own money.
Vaccination protects the person and also others, as it reduces the spread of disease. So it gives social benefits too.

options: work more days and learn better
quiz.why: Healthy workers work more days, are more productive and learn better.

questions.q: Human capital means…
options: skills, knowledge and health of people
questions.why: Human capital means the skills, knowledge and health of people.

questions.q: Most important source of human capital:
questions.why: Education is the most important source of human capital formation.

questions.q: RTE Act covers ages…
questions.why: The Right to Education Act covers children aged 6 to 14.

questions.q: AICTE regulates…
questions.why: AICTE regulates technical education in India.

questions.q: Human capital is…
questions.why: Human capital is intangible, since it is in the people and cannot be seen or touched. Physical capital is tangible.

questions.q: Kothari Commission recommended education spending of…
questions.why: The Kothari Commission (1964–66) recommended spending 6% of GDP on education.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Migration is a source of human capital formation. Reason (R): People migrate for better jobs, raising their productivity and earnings.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. People move for better jobs, which raises their skills, productivity and earnings, so migration helps form human capital.

questions.q: Human development views education as…
questions.why: The human development view takes education as an end in itself, because it improves people's lives directly.

questions.q: Case: A firm sends engineers to a 3-month course abroad. Source?
questions.why: Training provided by a firm to its own engineers is on-the-job training, a source of human capital.

questions.q: Case: GDP ₹250 lakh crore; education spending 4%. Amount?
questions.why: 4% of ₹250 lakh crore = 0.04 × 250 = ₹10 lakh crore.

questions.q: Which is NOT a difference between physical and human capital?
options: Human capital is inseparable from owner
questions.why: The false statement is that both are intangible. Physical capital is tangible, whereas human capital is intangible.

questions.q: Case: 2,000 workers lose 6 days each to illness; programme cuts loss by half. Workdays gained?
questions.why: Illness costs 2,000 × 6 = 12,000 workdays. Cutting the loss by half saves 12,000 ÷ 2 = 6,000 workdays.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Government must invest in education. Reason (R): Benefits of education spread to society and the poor may not afford it.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Education benefits all of society, and the poor may not be able to pay for it, so the government should invest.

questions.q: Case: A state says it funds schools “so that every child can live a fuller life”. Which view?
questions.why: Funding schools so that every child can live a fuller life treats education as valuable in itself. This is the human development view.

questions.q: Case: Literacy 2001 ≈ 65% and 2011 ≈ 74%. Change?
questions.why: Literacy rose from about 65% to 74%, which is a rise of about 9 percentage points. A change in a percentage is stated in percentage points.

questions.q: NEP 2020 recommends public education spending of…
questions.why: NEP 2020 recommends that public spending on education should reach 6% of GDP.

courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

courses.title: IED Ch 5 · Rural Development
courses.summary: Meaning of rural development, rural credit (institutional sources, NABARD, SHGs), agricultural marketing and government measures, alternative channels, diversification into allied and non-farm activities, and organic farming.
outcomes: Learners can describe sources and problems of rural credit
Learners can explain agricultural marketing measures and alternative channels
Learners can explain diversification with examples
Learners can evaluate organic farming

scenes.text: Bhola needs ₹20,000 for seeds; the moneylender charges 5% a month.
One bad harvest and the debt doubles.
Institutional credit and self-help groups offer a way out.

steps.title: Meaning of rural development
steps.body: Action plans for the economic and social development of areas left behind: human resources (literacy, especially female; health and sanitation), land reforms, infrastructure (electricity, irrigation, credit, marketing, roads, research), and poverty alleviation. About two-thirds of Indians still live in rural areas.

steps.title: Sources of rural credit
steps.body:
- **Non-institutional**: moneylenders, traders, landlords, relatives — often high interest and exploitation.
- **Institutional**: **commercial banks** (nationalisation 1969 and social banking), **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** (from 1975), **cooperative credit societies**, and **NABARD** (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development, **1982**) as apex body coordinating rural finance.
- **Self-Help Groups (SHGs)**: 15–20 members (mostly women) save small amounts regularly, lend to members; banks lend to SHGs (SHG–bank linkage). This is **microcredit**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Interest comparison
steps.body: Loan ₹20,000 for 6 months. Moneylender 5% per month simple interest → interest = 20,000 × 5% × 6 = **₹6,000**. Bank at 7% per year → interest = 20,000 × 7% × 0.5 = **₹700**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: SHG
steps.body: 20 women each save ₹200 a month → ₹4,000 a month; after a year ₹48,000 pooled; bank lends 4× the corpus → **₹1,92,000** available for members’ small enterprises.

steps.title: Problems
steps.body: Institutional credit has not fully replaced moneylenders; limited reach; poor recovery and defaults; loans used for consumption; farm loan waivers debated; need for better credit to small and marginal farmers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying NABARD gives loans directly to every farmer — it is an apex refinance and coordination body.
- Forgetting SHGs mainly empower women and promote thrift.

activity.prompt: A farmer borrows ₹10,000 from a moneylender at 4% per month (simple interest) for 5 months. Interest payable (₹)?

quiz.why: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was set up in 1982.
Self-help groups (SHGs) in rural areas mostly have women members, who save together and lend among themselves.
A moneylender is a non-institutional (informal) source of credit. Banks, RRBs and NABARD are institutional.
Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were set up from 1975 to give credit to rural areas.
Microcredit means small loans to the poor, and it is linked with self-help groups.

scenes.text: Lakshmi sells tomatoes to the first trader who comes, at whatever price he offers.
The scales are faulty; she gets no market information.
Better marketing systems can change that.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Agricultural marketing** includes assembling, storage, processing, transportation, packaging, grading and distribution of farm produce. Problems: faulty weights, lack of market information, distress sales, lack of storage, many middlemen.

steps.title: Government measures
steps.body:
- **Regulated markets** (APMC): orderly and transparent marketing; licensed traders, standard weights.
- **Physical infrastructure**: roads, railways, warehouses, cold storage, processing units.
- **Cooperative marketing**: farmers pool produce to get better prices (e.g., milk cooperatives in Gujarat).
- **Policy instruments**: **Minimum Support Price (MSP)** for major crops, **buffer stocks** of wheat and rice maintained by the **Food Corporation of India (FCI)**, and the **Public Distribution System (PDS)** for subsidised food grains to the poor.
- Digital platforms like e-NAM for online trading.

steps.title: Alternative marketing channels
steps.body: Farmers selling directly to consumers: **Apni Mandi** (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan), **Hadaspar Mandi** (Pune), **Rythu Bazars** (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana), **Uzhavar Sandies** (Tamil Nadu); and contracts with national/international food chains and organised retail.

steps.title: Solved example 1: MSP effect
steps.body: MSP of wheat ₹2,400 per quintal; open market price falls to ₹2,100. A farmer selling 50 quintals to the government gets ₹1,20,000 instead of ₹1,05,000 → **₹15,000** protection.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Fewer middlemen
steps.body: Consumer pays ₹40/kg for tomatoes; farmer got ₹15/kg through three middlemen. Selling at a Rythu Bazar at ₹30/kg: farmer gains ₹15/kg and consumer saves ₹10/kg.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing MSP (price floor for farmers) with PDS issue prices (for consumers).
- Saying buffer stocks are kept by private traders — FCI holds them.

activity.prompt: Match the alternative market with its state

quiz.why: The minimum support price (MSP) protects farmers from a fall in prices by setting a floor.
Buffer stocks of grains are maintained by the Food Corporation of India (FCI).
The Public Distribution System (PDS) provides subsidised food grains to people.
Regulated markets aim at ensuring fair and transparent trade, to protect farmers from exploitation.
Rythu Bazars are farmers' markets in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, where farmers sell directly to consumers.

scenes.text: A family in Gujarat earns extra income from two buffaloes.
Their cousins in Kerala run a fish pond; another runs a mobile repair shop.
Diversification spreads risk and creates jobs.

steps.title: Why diversify?
steps.body: Agriculture is risky (monsoon dependence) and already over-crowded. Diversification means (a) changing the **cropping pattern** (food grains → horticulture, cash crops) and (b) shifting workers to **allied and non-farm activities**.

steps.title: Allied and non-farm activities
steps.body:
- **Animal husbandry**: cattle, goats, poultry. **Operation Flood** (launched 1970 by the National Dairy Development Board; led by Dr Verghese Kurien) made India the world’s largest milk producer.
- **Fisheries**: inland (rivers, ponds) and marine; women do much of the processing and marketing.
- **Horticulture**: fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, plantation crops — high value; often called the “**Golden Revolution**” period of horticulture growth.
- **Non-farm**: agro-processing, food processing, handicrafts, tourism, IT kiosks/common service centres, construction.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Income spread
steps.body: A farmer earns ₹60,000 from crops; adding dairy (₹36,000) and poultry (₹12,000) raises income to **₹1,08,000** and protects against a bad monsoon.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Identify activity
steps.body: Floriculture near cities → horticulture. Milk cooperative → animal husbandry. Running a food-processing unit making pickles → non-farm (agro-processing).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Operation Flood was about irrigation — it is dairy.
- Treating diversification as abandoning agriculture.

activity.prompt: Which diversification?

quiz.why: Operation Flood was the programme for increasing milk production, so it relates to dairy.
Horticulture is the growing of fruits, vegetables and flowers.
Diversification is needed because agriculture is risky and over-crowded, so people need other sources of income.
Food processing is a non-farm activity, as it is done outside the field.

quiz.q: Golden Revolution refers to growth in…
quiz.why: The Golden Revolution refers to the growth of horticulture in India.

scenes.text: Years of chemical fertiliser use left Ramesh’s soil hard and less fertile.
He switches to compost, crop rotation and natural pest control.
Organic produce fetches a higher price in city markets.

steps.title: Organic farming
steps.body:
A whole system of farming that restores and enhances ecological balance; avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides; uses compost, green manure, crop rotation, biological pest control.

**Benefits**: substitutes costly inputs with local ones, generates income from premium prices and exports, healthier food, more labour-intensive (jobs), environment-friendly.
**Challenges**: lower yields initially, needs awareness and certification, marketing support, shorter shelf life of produce.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Price premium
steps.body: Regular vegetables ₹30/kg; organic ₹45/kg. Yield drops from 1,000 kg to 900 kg. Revenue: regular ₹30,000; organic ₹40,500 → **₹10,500** more (before certification costs).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Sustainability
steps.body: Overuse of groundwater in Punjab’s paddy cycle lowers water tables; crop diversification and water-saving methods are part of sustainable rural development.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying organic farming always gives higher yields — often yields dip at first.
- Forgetting certification and marketing needs.

statements.s: Organic farming avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides.
Organic yields are always higher from the first year.
Organic farming tends to be labour-intensive.
Organic produce has a longer shelf life than conventional.

quiz.why: Organic farming uses compost, manure and natural methods of pest control, and avoids chemical inputs.
A benefit of organic farming is that organic products can fetch premium prices.

options: lower initial yields and certification needs
quiz.why: A challenge of organic farming is lower yields at the start and the need for certification.

options: using resources so future generations can also meet needs
quiz.why: Sustainable development means using resources so that future generations can also meet their needs.

quiz.q: Falling water tables are linked with…
quiz.why: Falling water tables are linked with overuse (over-extraction) of groundwater.

questions.q: NABARD was set up in…
questions.why: NABARD was set up in 1982.

questions.q: Operation Flood relates to…
questions.why: Operation Flood is the dairy programme that increased milk production in India.

questions.q: MSP stands for…
questions.why: MSP stands for Minimum Support Price, the price at which the government buys crops.

questions.q: Buffer stocks are held by…
questions.why: Buffer stocks are held by the Food Corporation of India (FCI).

questions.q: SHGs promote…
questions.why: Self-help groups promote thrift (saving) and microcredit among members.

questions.q: Uzhavar Sandies are in…
questions.why: Uzhavar Sandies are farmers' markets in Tamil Nadu.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Diversification reduces risk for rural households. Reason (R): Income comes from several activities, not only monsoon-dependent crops.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. If income comes from several activities, a bad monsoon does not hurt as much, so risk falls.

questions.q: Case: Moneylender loan ₹15,000 at 3% per month for 8 months. Interest?
questions.why: Interest = principal × rate × time = ₹15,000 × 0.03 × 8 = ₹3,600.

questions.q: Which is an alternative marketing channel in Pune?
questions.why: Hadaspar Mandi is an alternative marketing channel in Pune. Rythu Bazar is in Andhra Pradesh, Uzhavar Sandy in Tamil Nadu and Apni Mandi in Punjab.

questions.q: Case: MSP ₹2,000/quintal; market price ₹1,800. Gain on 40 quintals sold at MSP?
questions.why: The gain per quintal is ₹2,000 − ₹1,800 = ₹200. On 40 quintals it is 200 × 40 = ₹8,000.

questions.q: Which is NOT a part of rural development?
questions.why: Urban stock market reform is not about rural development. Land reforms, poverty alleviation and rural infrastructure are.

questions.q: Case: 15 women save ₹300 each per month in an SHG. Total savings in 1 year?
questions.why: 15 members × ₹300 × 12 months = ₹54,000.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Institutional credit has completely replaced moneylenders. Reason (R): Banks and cooperatives expanded after 1969.
questions.why: The assertion is false, since moneylenders still exist. The reason is true, as banks and cooperatives expanded after 1969.

questions.q: Case: A farmer’s yield falls 10% after going organic but price rises 50%. Revenue change (old revenue = 100)?
questions.why: Yield falls to 0.9 and price rises to 1.5, so revenue = 0.9 × 1.5 = 1.35 times the old, which is a rise of 35%.

questions.q: Regional Rural Banks were set up from…
questions.why: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were set up from 1975.

questions.q: Case: A village switches part of its paddy land to vegetables and starts a dairy. This is…
questions.why: Moving some paddy land to vegetables and starting a dairy spreads income over more activities. This is diversification.
