courses.title: IED Ch 6 · Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
courses.summary: Who is a worker, worker–population ratio, self-employed, casual and regular workers, employment by sector and jobless growth, informalisation, types of unemployment and government programmes like MGNREGA.
outcomes: Learners can compute WPR and unemployment rate
Learners can classify workers by status and sector
Learners can explain informalisation and its effects
Learners can explain types of unemployment and policy responses

scenes.text: Sunita works on her family farm without wages.
Her brother is a plumber on daily wages; her cousin is a salaried clerk.
All three are workers — even unpaid family helpers.

steps.title: Who is a worker?
steps.body: A **worker** is anyone engaged in an economic activity that contributes to the gross domestic product, including self-employed and unpaid helpers in family enterprises. Those temporarily absent due to illness are also counted. Students, homemakers (doing only domestic work), retired people are not counted as workers.

steps.title: Worker–population ratio (WPR)
steps.body: **WPR = (Number of workers ÷ Total population) × 100**. It shows the share of the population actively contributing to production. In India, WPR is higher in rural than urban areas (more people needed in farming; urban people often study longer) and higher for men than women. Official data come from the **Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)** by NSO.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Compute WPR
steps.body: A village of 2,000 people has 760 workers → WPR = 760/2,000 × 100 = **38%**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why lower female WPR?
steps.body: Women’s unpaid domestic work is not counted; social norms, safety and lack of suitable jobs reduce paid work → female WPR appears lower than male.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Excluding unpaid family helpers from workers.
- Counting full-time students as workers.

activity.prompt: A town of 50,000 people has 17,500 workers. What is the worker–population ratio (%)?

quiz.q: An unpaid helper on a family farm is…
quiz.why: An unpaid helper on a family farm contributes to output, so is counted as a worker.
Worker–population ratio (WPR) = (number of workers ÷ total population) × 100.
WPR is generally higher in rural areas, as more people, including women and family helpers, are in work there.

quiz.q: Employment data in India come from…
quiz.why: Employment data come from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) of the NSO.
A full-time college student is not engaged in economic activity, so is not counted as a worker.

scenes.text: Ravi owns an auto-rickshaw and drives it himself.
His neighbour works on construction sites, paid daily, sometimes without work for days.
His sister has a monthly salary with provident fund.

steps.title: Status of workers
steps.body:
- **Self-employed**: own and operate an enterprise (farmers on own land, shopkeepers, auto owners). The largest category in India, especially in rural areas.
- **Casual wage labourers**: hired on daily/periodic contracts, no job security or social security (construction, farm labour).
- **Regular salaried employees**: hired on a regular basis, paid regularly, often with social security benefits.

Urban areas have a higher share of regular salaried workers than rural areas; women are more often self-employed or casual.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) A tailor running her own shop → self-employed. (b) A farm labourer paid ₹400 per day → casual. (c) A bank clerk → regular salaried.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Distribution
steps.body: Of 100 rural workers: 57 self-employed, 25 casual, 18 regular (illustrative) → majority depend on own enterprise; few have job security.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a daily-wage worker “self-employed”.
- Assuming all self-employed people are well-off — many are small farmers or vendors.

activity.prompt: Status of worker

quiz.q: Largest category of workers in India:
quiz.why: The largest category of workers in India is the self-employed.
Casual workers are hired on a daily basis, so usually lack job security and social security.

quiz.q: Regular salaried jobs are more common in…
quiz.why: Regular salaried jobs are more common in urban areas than in rural areas.
An auto owner-driver runs his own enterprise, so is self-employed.
A farm worker paid daily is hired on a casual basis, so is a casual worker.

lessons.title: Employment across sectors and its changing structure

scenes.text: In 1950 most workers were in agriculture.
Today services contribute over half of GDP, yet agriculture still employs the largest share of workers.
Output shifted faster than jobs.

steps.title: Sectors
steps.body:
- **Primary**: agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining.
- **Secondary**: manufacturing, construction, electricity, gas and water supply.
- **Tertiary (services)**: trade, transport, communication, finance, real estate, public administration, education, health.

In India, the **primary sector still employs the largest share** of workers (though falling), while the **services sector contributes the largest share of GDP**. Women are more concentrated in primary activities.

steps.title: Growth and jobless growth
steps.body: From the 1950s, GDP grew faster than employment, especially after 1990s → **jobless growth**: output rose without a proportionate rise in jobs. Structural change in employment has been slow.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Share vs output
steps.body: Suppose agriculture employs 45% of workers but produces 18% of GDP → output per worker is low → disguised unemployment likely.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Employment elasticity
steps.body: GDP grows 7%, employment grows 1.5% → employment elasticity ≈ 1.5/7 ≈ **0.21** → each 1% growth adds only 0.21% jobs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying services employ most workers in India.
- Confusing share of GDP with share of employment.

activity.prompt: GDP grows 8% and employment grows 2%. What is the employment elasticity?

quiz.why: The primary sector (agriculture) employs the largest number of workers in India.
The services sector is the largest contributor to India's GDP.
Jobless growth means GDP grows faster than employment.
Construction is a secondary sector activity, as it builds structures from materials.
Banking is a service, so it belongs to the tertiary sector.

scenes.text: A delivery rider works 10 hours a day through an app.
He has no fixed salary, no paid leave and no pension.
Most Indian workers are in the informal sector.

steps.title: Formal and informal sector
steps.body:
- **Formal (organised) sector**: public sector establishments and private establishments employing **10 or more** hired workers; workers get social security (PF, gratuity, pension), regular salary, legal protection, right to form unions.
- **Informal (unorganised) sector**: farmers, farm labourers, small enterprise owners and their workers, self-employed with no hired workers, casual workers — no regular income, no social security, little protection.
- A large majority (over 90% by many estimates) of India’s workforce is informal.

steps.title: Informalisation and policy
steps.body: Since the 1980s, a rising share of jobs has been informal (even within formal firms through contract labour). Government steps: social security schemes for unorganised workers, e-Shram portal registration, skill programmes, labour codes consolidating laws, and support to micro enterprises.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Classify
steps.body: (a) A government school teacher → formal. (b) A worker in a 6-person tailoring unit → informal. (c) A contract cleaner in a big company paid daily without PF → informal job within a formal firm.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Effect of a shock
steps.body: During a lockdown, informal workers without savings or social security face immediate income loss → need for safety nets.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming all jobs in big companies are formal.
- Forgetting the 10-workers threshold for private formal establishments.

activity.prompt: Formal or informal?

items.text: Factory worker with PF in a 200-worker plant

quiz.q: Private formal establishments employ at least…
quiz.why: A private formal establishment is one with 10 or more workers.
Informal workers usually lack social security benefits such as provident fund and pension.
Most Indian workers are in the informal sector, with no secure job or benefits.

quiz.q: Contract labour without benefits in a big firm is…
quiz.why: Contract labour in a big firm without benefits is informal employment, even though the firm is formal.
The e-Shram portal registers unorganised (informal) workers.

story.title: Five brothers on one small farm

scenes.text: Five brothers work on a farm that needs only three.
If two leave, output stays the same.
They are disguisedly unemployed.

steps.title: Meaning and types
steps.body:
**Unemployment**: people who are willing and able to work at the prevailing wage but do not find work.

- **Open unemployment**: clearly without work (common in urban areas among educated youth).
- **Disguised unemployment**: more people working than needed; marginal productivity ≈ zero (common in agriculture).
- **Seasonal unemployment**: no work in certain seasons (farm workers after harvest).
- **Educated unemployment** and **frictional** (between jobs) also discussed.

steps.title: Government programmes
steps.body:
- **Direct job creation**: public works (roads, canals), public sector jobs.
- **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005**: guarantees **100 days** of wage employment per year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work.
- **Indirect**: faster growth, self-employment schemes (e.g., PMEGP), skill programmes (Skill India, PMKVY), rural livelihood missions (NRLM).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Disguised unemployment
steps.body: Farm output with 5 workers = 100 quintals; with 3 workers also 100 quintals → **2 workers** are disguisedly unemployed (marginal product zero).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Unemployment rate
steps.body: Labour force 800 (employed + unemployed seeking work); unemployed 40 → **unemployment rate = 40/800 × 100 = 5%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing unemployed by total population (use labour force).
- Saying MGNREGA guarantees jobs to every individual for a year — it is 100 days per rural household.

activity.prompt: Labour force 1,200; unemployed 54. Unemployment rate (%)?

quiz.why: Disguised unemployment is common in agriculture, where more people work on the farm than are needed.

options: 100 days of wage work per rural household per year
quiz.why: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of wage work in a year to each rural household that asks for it.
The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed as a percentage of the labour force.

quiz.q: Work available only during harvest causes…
quiz.why: Work that is available only in the harvest season causes seasonal unemployment.
MGNREGA was enacted in 2005.

questions.q: A worker contributes to…
questions.why: A worker takes part in economic activity, so contributes to GDP.

questions.q: Largest category of workers in India:
questions.why: The self-employed are the largest category of workers in India.

questions.q: MGNREGA provides…
options: 100 days of work per rural household
questions.why: MGNREGA provides 100 days of wage work per rural household in a year.

questions.q: Disguised unemployment means marginal productivity is…
questions.why: In disguised unemployment, extra workers add little or nothing to output, so their marginal productivity is zero or near zero.

questions.q: WPR is the ratio of workers to…
questions.why: WPR is the ratio of workers to the total population, expressed as a percentage.

questions.q: Formal private establishments employ…
questions.why: A private formal establishment is one that employs 10 or more workers.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Services contribute most to GDP but agriculture employs most workers. Reason (R): Structural change in employment has lagged behind output.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Output has moved toward services, but employment has stayed in agriculture, so structural change in jobs lags behind output.

questions.q: Case: Population 4,000; workers 1,520. WPR?
Case: Labour force 600; unemployed 30. Unemployment rate?
questions.why: Unemployment rate = (30 ÷ 600) × 100 = 5%.

questions.q: Which is informal work?
questions.why: A domestic worker has no formal contract and no social security, so the work is informal. The others are formal jobs.

questions.q: Case: GDP grows 6%, employment 0.9%. Employment elasticity?
questions.why: Employment elasticity = growth of employment ÷ growth of GDP = 0.9 ÷ 6 = 0.15.

questions.q: Case: A family farm produces the same output with 4 or 7 workers. Disguised unemployment?
questions.why: The same output is produced with 4 workers, so the extra 7 − 4 = 3 workers are disguised unemployed.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Female WPR appears low in India. Reason (R): Much of women’s work is unpaid domestic work not counted as economic activity.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Much of women's unpaid domestic work is not counted as economic activity, so the female WPR looks low.

questions.q: Case: Workers in a car plant hired through contractors without PF. Their employment is…
questions.why: Workers hired through contractors without PF have no job security or benefits, so their work is informal.

questions.q: Jobless growth means…
questions.why: Jobless growth means output grows faster than the number of jobs.

questions.q: Case: Rural workers idle from April to June after harvest. Type?
questions.why: Rural workers idle for a few months after harvest face seasonal unemployment.

courses.title: IED Ch 7 · Environment and Sustainable Development
courses.summary: Functions of the environment, carrying and absorptive capacity, the state of India’s environment, global warming and ozone depletion, the meaning of sustainable development and strategies for India.
outcomes: Learners can explain the four functions of environment
Learners can describe India’s environmental problems and CPCB
Learners can distinguish global warming from ozone depletion
Learners can propose strategies for sustainable development

lessons.title: Environment: functions, carrying and absorptive capacity

story.title: The river that could not clean itself

scenes.text: A river near a town once cleaned itself of the little waste it received.
As factories grew, waste poured in faster than the river could absorb.
Fish died — the river’s absorptive capacity was exceeded.

steps.title: Meaning and functions
steps.body:
**Environment** is the total planetary inheritance — all **biotic** (living: plants, animals, birds) and **abiotic** (non-living: air, water, land) factors that influence each other.

Four functions:
1. **Supplies resources** — renewable (forests, fish) and non-renewable (fossil fuels).
2. **Assimilates waste**.
3. **Sustains life** through genetic and biodiversity.
4. **Provides aesthetic services** (scenery).

steps.title: Carrying and absorptive capacity
steps.body:
- **Carrying capacity**: resource extraction should not exceed regeneration, and waste should be within absorptive capacity.
- **Absorptive capacity**: ability of the environment to absorb degradation.
- When these are exceeded → **environmental crisis**: resources become scarce and pollution rises; costs of fixing it (opportunity costs, health costs) increase. Today the demand for environmental resources exceeds supply — a reversal of the earlier situation.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the function
steps.body: (a) Timber for furniture → supplies resources. (b) Soil breaking down organic waste → assimilates waste. (c) A sanctuary preserving tigers → sustains life (biodiversity). (d) Tourists viewing the Himalayas → aesthetic services.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Carrying capacity
steps.body: A forest regrows 1,000 trees a year. Cutting 1,500 a year exceeds carrying capacity → forest shrinks over time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating renewable resources as unlimited — overuse can exhaust them.
- Confusing carrying capacity with absorptive capacity.

activity.prompt: Match the environmental function

quiz.why: Abiotic elements are the non-living parts of the environment, such as air and water. Plants, birds and insects are biotic.
When use of the environment goes beyond its absorptive capacity, it can no longer absorb waste, so pollution and crisis result.

options: replenished over time if not overused
quiz.why: Renewable resources such as forests, fish and water can regenerate naturally, so they last if we use them within their rate of regeneration. 'Never exhausted' is wrong because overuse can still exhaust them; fossil fuels and metals are non-renewable.

quiz.q: Biodiversity relates to the function of…
quiz.why: Biodiversity, the variety of living things, keeps ecosystems working: it supports food, clean air and water, and soil health. This life-support role is why it matters beyond looks or beauty.

quiz.q: Carrying capacity requires extraction to be…
quiz.why: Carrying capacity means the environment can support its use only if resource extraction stays within the rate at which resources regenerate. If extraction is higher than regeneration, resources decline and the capacity is exceeded.

scenes.text: Winter air in many north Indian cities becomes hazardous.
Overgrazing and deforestation degrade land.
Habitats shrink for many species.

steps.title: Key problems
steps.body:
- **Land degradation**: deforestation, shifting cultivation, encroachment, forest fires, overgrazing, poor soil conservation, improper crop rotation, overuse of chemicals, poor irrigation management (waterlogging, salinity).
- **Loss of biodiversity**.
- **Air pollution**: vehicles and industry in cities; crop-residue burning; dust.
- **Water pollution and scarcity**: untreated sewage and industrial waste in rivers; groundwater depletion.
- **Solid waste** and plastic, e-waste.

Pressure arises from a large population and growing affluent consumption.

steps.title: Institutions
steps.body: The **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)**, set up in **1974**, and State Pollution Control Boards monitor and regulate pollution, collect data on air and water quality and enforce standards. India’s National Clean Air Programme (2019) targets reductions in particulate pollution in many cities.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the cause
steps.body: (a) Fields becoming salty after excess canal irrigation → poor irrigation management. (b) Hills losing soil after forest cutting → deforestation. (c) City air thick with particulates from vehicles and burning → air pollution.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Opportunity cost
steps.body: A city spends crores on water purification because its river is polluted; that money could have built schools → environmental degradation has **opportunity costs**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Blaming only poverty — affluent consumption also strains the environment.
- Forgetting that CPCB was set up in 1974.

activity.prompt: Which problem?

quiz.why: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) was set up in 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act. 1986 is the year of the Environment Protection Act, which is the tempting wrong choice.
Overgrazing strips the plant cover so soil erodes and the land loses fertility. Solar panels, organic farming and rainwater harvesting protect land and resources rather than degrade them.

quiz.q: Pressure on the environment comes from…
quiz.why: Environmental pressure has two sources: the growing number of people (population) and the high consumption of affluent households and nations. Neither alone explains it, so both matter.

options: money spent on cleaning that could fund other uses
quiz.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best use given up. Money spent cleaning up pollution could have funded schools or health instead, so that foregone alternative is the cost of pollution.
Too much canal irrigation raises the water table and leaves salts on the surface, causing waterlogging and salinity. These degrade the soil and cut crop yields, which is land degradation, not a gain.

scenes.text: Glaciers are retreating; heatwaves are more frequent.
Scientists link this to rising greenhouse gases.
Some environmental problems cross all borders.

steps.title: Global warming
steps.body: A gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth’s lower atmosphere due to rising **greenhouse gases** (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide) from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and some farming practices. Effects: melting ice and glaciers, sea-level rise, extreme weather, threats to agriculture, water and health. Global agreements include the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992) and the **Paris Agreement (2015)**.

steps.title: Ozone depletion
steps.body: The **ozone layer** in the stratosphere protects us from harmful ultraviolet rays. It is depleted by **chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)** and other chemicals (used earlier in refrigerators, aerosols). The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phased out these substances; the ozone layer is slowly recovering.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Cause and effect
steps.body: Burning coal for electricity → more CO₂ → stronger greenhouse effect → higher temperatures → more heatwaves and erratic monsoons → crop losses.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Policy success
steps.body: Ban on CFCs after the Montreal Protocol → ozone-depleting substances fell → the ozone layer is recovering → an example of effective global cooperation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing global warming (greenhouse gases) with ozone depletion (CFCs, UV rays).
- Thinking ozone near the ground is protective — ground-level ozone is a pollutant.

statements.s: CFCs deplete the ozone layer.
Global warming is caused mainly by CFCs only.
The Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987.
The ozone layer protects us from UV rays.

quiz.why: Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels is the major greenhouse gas that traps heat. Nitrogen, oxygen and argon make up most of the air but do not trap heat significantly.

quiz.q: Ozone layer is damaged mainly by…
quiz.why: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), once used in refrigerators and aerosols, release chlorine in the stratosphere that breaks down ozone. Helium, water vapour and oxygen do not deplete the ozone layer.

The Montreal Protocol, agreed in 1987, committed countries to phase out ozone-depleting substances like CFCs. 1992 and 2015 are dates of other environmental agreements, which are the tempting wrong choices.

quiz.q: A likely effect of global warming:
quiz.why: Global warming melts glaciers and ice sheets and warms ocean water, which makes it expand, so sea levels rise. More ice or cooler summers everywhere would be the opposite of warming.
The Paris Agreement on climate change was adopted in 2015, aiming to limit global warming. 1997 (Kyoto) and 1987 (Montreal) are other treaties, not this one.

scenes.text: A village installs solar pumps and biogas plants.
Delhi switched its buses to CNG.
These are steps toward sustainable development.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: The **Brundtland Commission (1987)** defined sustainable development as development that **meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**. Herman Daly suggested: limit population to carrying capacity; technological progress should be input-efficient, not input-consuming; renewable resources extracted sustainably; non-renewable depletion should not exceed the rate of creation of renewable substitutes; pollution should be corrected.

steps.title: Strategies for India
steps.body:
- **Non-conventional energy**: solar, wind, small (mini/micro) hydel plants.
- **LPG and gobar gas** in rural areas to replace firewood and dung cakes.
- **CNG** for public transport in cities (Delhi is a well-known example).
- **Wind power**; **solar power through photovoltaic cells**.
- **Traditional knowledge and practices** (Ayurveda, traditional water harvesting, herbal products).
- **Biocomposting** (compost, earthworms), **biopest control** (neem-based pesticides, birds and natural predators).

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the strategy
steps.body: (a) A farmer uses neem-based spray instead of chemicals → biopest control. (b) A village uses cow-dung biogas for cooking → gobar gas. (c) A city bus fleet on CNG → cleaner urban transport.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Cost comparison
steps.body: A family spends ₹1,200/month on diesel for an irrigation pump. A solar pump costs ₹60,000 (with subsidy) and saves fuel cost → payback ≈ **50 months**, then near-free power for years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Misquoting the Brundtland definition.
- Thinking sustainable development means no development.

activity.prompt: Sustainable habits you can adopt
items: Switch off lights and fans when leaving
Use public transport or cycle for short trips
Save water while brushing and bathing
Plant and care for a tree

quiz.q: The Brundtland Commission report was in…
quiz.why: The Brundtland Commission's report 'Our Common Future' came out in 1987 and popularised the idea of sustainable development. 1992 is the Earth Summit year, a tempting but different event.

quiz.q: Using neem spray instead of chemicals is…
quiz.why: Neem spray replaces chemical pesticides with a natural plant-based one, which is biopest control. CNG is a fuel, hydel is water power and biocomposting turns waste into manure.

quiz.q: CNG for buses was adopted notably in…
quiz.why: Delhi moved its buses to CNG (compressed natural gas) to cut air pollution, following court orders around the late 1990s and early 2000s. The other places named are not noted for this switch.

options: meeting present needs without harming future generations
quiz.why: Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs. It does not mean stopping growth, nor using up all resources now.
A solar photovoltaic cell turns sunlight directly into electricity. It does not make fuel from water or turn coal into gas, and it is not driven by wind.

questions.q: Environment includes biotic and…
questions.why: The environment includes living (biotic) things like plants, animals and humans, together with non-living (abiotic) things like air, water and soil. 'Only animals' or 'only plants' leaves out half of it.

questions.q: Sustainable development definition comes from…
questions.why: The Brundtland Commission (World Commission on Environment and Development) defined sustainable development in its 1987 report. The Finance, Planning and Kothari Commissions deal with other subjects.

questions.q: CFCs damage…
questions.why: CFCs release chlorine that destroys ozone molecules in the stratosphere, thinning the ozone layer that shields us from UV rays. They are not mainly harmful to soil, forests or rivers.

questions.q: CPCB was set up in…
questions.why: India's Central Pollution Control Board was set up in 1974. 1987 and 2015 belong to the Montreal Protocol/Brundtland report and the Paris Agreement, so they are tempting but wrong.

questions.q: Which is a function of environment?
questions.why: One of the environment's functions is to supply resources such as water, minerals and timber. Setting taxes, printing money and building roads are done by governments and banks, not by the environment.

questions.q: Exceeding absorptive capacity results in…
questions.why: Absorptive capacity is the environment's ability to take in waste and pollution. When waste exceeds it, pollution builds up and an environmental crisis follows, rather than less pollution.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Global warming is linked to burning fossil fuels. Reason (R): Fossil fuels release greenhouse gases like CO₂.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true: burning fossil fuels releases CO₂ and other greenhouse gases that trap heat, causing global warming. The reason directly explains the assertion.

questions.q: Gobar gas is used mainly in…
questions.why: Gobar gas (biogas) is made from cattle dung and used for cooking and lighting in rural areas, where cattle and dung are easily available.

questions.q: Case: A village cuts 2,000 trees/year while only 1,200 regrow. This violates…
questions.why: The village removes 2,000 trees a year but only 1,200 regrow, so extraction exceeds regeneration. That breaks the carrying capacity rule that use must stay within regeneration.

questions.q: Case: A farmer uses earthworms to make compost. Strategy?
questions.why: Using earthworms to turn waste into compost is biocomposting (vermicompost). CNG is a fuel, hydel power comes from water and biopest control uses natural pest controls.

questions.q: The Montreal Protocol addressed…
questions.why: The Montreal Protocol (1987) is an international agreement to phase out ozone-depleting substances like CFCs. It is not about fisheries, trade tariffs or nuclear weapons.

questions.q: Which is NOT a strategy for sustainable development?
questions.why: Burning crop residue releases smoke and greenhouse gases and harms air quality, so it is not sustainable. Solar energy, water harvesting and mini hydel plants use renewable, low-pollution methods.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ground-level ozone protects humans from UV rays. Reason (R): Stratospheric ozone absorbs UV radiation.
questions.why: The assertion is false: ground-level ozone is a pollutant that harms health. The reason is true: ozone high in the stratosphere absorbs UV, so only that ozone protects us.

questions.q: Case: A city spends ₹500 crore yearly treating polluted river water. The cost is an example of…
questions.why: Spending ₹500 crore a year on cleaning a polluted river is money that could have been used elsewhere, so it is the opportunity cost of environmental degradation. It is not a tax, profit or subsidy.

questions.q: Case: Herman Daly’s rule says depletion of non-renewables should not exceed…
options: rate of creation of renewable substitutes
questions.why: Herman Daly's rule says non-renewable resources should be used no faster than renewable substitutes can be created. Growth, inflation or population rates are not the benchmark.

questions.q: Case: Diesel pump cost ₹1,500/month; a ₹45,000 solar pump replaces it. Payback period?
questions.why: Payback period = cost ÷ monthly saving = 45,000 ÷ 1,500 = 30 months. The solar pump recovers its cost in 30 months by saving the diesel expense.

courses.title: IED Ch 8 · Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
courses.summary: Development paths of India, China and Pakistan: planning starts, China’s Great Leap Forward, Cultural Revolution and 1978 reforms, Pakistan’s strategy, and comparison of demographic, growth, sectoral and human development indicators.
outcomes: Learners can compare the development paths of the three countries
Learners can explain China’s pre- and post-1978 policies
Learners can describe Pakistan’s strategy and problems
Learners can compare key indicators and draw lessons

lessons.title: Three neighbours, three paths: a timeline

scenes.text: India became independent in 1947.
Pakistan was created in 1947.
The People’s Republic of China was established in 1949. All three began planning around the same time.

steps.title: Similar starts
steps.body:
All three began their development journeys at about the same time with similar challenges: large populations, poverty, low industrial base. All adopted **planning**:

- **India**: First Five Year Plan **1951–56**.
- **China**: First Five Year Plan **1953**.
- **Pakistan**: First Five Year Plan (Medium Term Plan) **1956**.

India and Pakistan followed a **mixed economy** with a large public sector; China followed a **command (communist) economy** in which the state owned and directed most production.

steps.title: Why compare neighbours?
steps.body: Regional groupings (SAARC, ASEAN, G-20, BRICS) and globalisation make it useful to understand neighbours’ strategies — to learn from successes and failures and to understand competition and trade.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Order the starts
steps.body: Pakistan created and India independent (1947) → PRC (1949) → India’s First Plan (1951) → China’s First Plan (1953) → Pakistan’s First Plan (1956).

steps.title: Solved example 2: Economic system
steps.body: India and Pakistan: private and public sectors coexist (mixed). China till 1978: collective ownership, communes, central plans (command economy).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying China’s first plan began in 1949 (that is the year of the PRC; the plan began in 1953).
- Calling Pakistan’s early economy socialist (it was mixed).

activity.prompt: Arrange these events

quiz.q: China’s First Five Year Plan began in…
quiz.why: China launched its First Five Year Plan in 1953, after the People's Republic was set up in 1949. India's started in 1951 and Pakistan's in 1956, which are the tempting wrong choices.

quiz.q: Pakistan’s First Five Year Plan began in…
quiz.why: Pakistan's First Five Year Plan began in 1956. India's was 1951 and China's was 1953, so 1956 is the latest of the three.
India and Pakistan chose a mixed economy, where both the public and private sectors operate. Command economy was China's model before 1978; barter and feudal are not economic systems they adopted.
The People's Republic of China was established in 1949 under the Communist Party. 1978 is when its market reforms began, a tempting but different event.

quiz.q: A regional grouping in South Asia is…
quiz.why: SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) groups South Asian countries. The EU is European, OPEC is for oil exporters and NATO is a military alliance.

story.title: From communes to the world’s factory

scenes.text: In 1958 Chinese villages were organised into communes for collective farming.
After 1978, farmers could sell surplus output and factories opened in special zones.
China became a manufacturing giant.

steps.title: Before 1978
steps.body:
- **Great Leap Forward (GLF)** campaign, **1958**: mass industrialisation; people encouraged to set up industries in backyards; **commune system** of collective cultivation in rural areas. Problems: a severe drought and famine; the Soviet Union withdrew its experts (1960) after a conflict.
- **Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966–76)**: students and professionals sent to work and learn from the countryside; disruption of education and economy.

steps.title: Reforms from 1978
steps.body:
Introduced in phases (Deng Xiaoping era):
- **Agriculture**: commune lands divided into plots allotted to households (household responsibility system); farmers kept income after paying taxes.
- **Industry and services**: private firms and **township and village enterprises** allowed; SOEs faced competition.
- **Dual pricing**: farmers and firms sold fixed quantities at state prices and the rest at market prices; gradually market prices grew.
- **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** to attract foreign investors.
- **One-child policy** (introduced 1979; relaxed in 2015–16) slowed population growth but led to an ageing population and skewed sex ratio.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the policy
steps.body: (a) Families get plots and keep surplus after tax → household responsibility system. (b) Factory sells 1,000 units at state price and the rest at market price → dual pricing. (c) Foreign firm sets up in Shenzhen with tax breaks → SEZ.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why rapid growth?
steps.body: Early investment in health, education and land reforms created a base; reforms added incentives, FDI and export manufacturing → very high growth for decades.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying China’s reforms began in 1991 (that was India).
- Confusing the Great Leap Forward (1958) with the Cultural Revolution (1966–76).

activity.prompt: Match China’s policies
pairs: Part at state price, rest at market price

quiz.why: China's Great Leap Forward began in 1958 to push rapid industrialisation, including backyard industry and communes. 1966 is the Cultural Revolution, a tempting wrong choice.
China began market-oriented reforms in 1978. 1949 was the founding of the PRC, and 1991 was when India started its reforms.

options: fixed quantity at state price, rest at market price
quiz.why: Under dual pricing, farmers and firms sold a fixed quota at the government-set price and sold the rest at the market price. It does not mean two plans, two currencies or double taxes.

quiz.q: A consequence of the one-child policy:
quiz.why: The one-child policy cut births, so over time there were fewer young people and more old people, giving an ageing population. It did not make the population younger or grow faster.
Communes were collective farms in China where land was farmed together and the output shared. They are not related to stock markets, foreign trade or private banks.

story.title: Mixed economy with ups and downs

scenes.text: Pakistan built industries behind tariff walls in the 1950s and 1960s.
The Green Revolution raised food output.
Policy swung between nationalisation and liberalisation.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
- **Mixed economy** with public and private sectors.
- **1950s–60s**: regulated industrialisation, **import substitution**; tariff protection for consumer goods industries; direct import controls.
- **Green Revolution**: mechanisation and more public investment in infrastructure → higher food grain output; changed agrarian structure.
- **1970s**: **nationalisation** of capital goods industries.
- **Late 1970s–80s**: shift toward denationalisation and encouragement of the private sector; financial support from Western nations and remittances from emigrants to the Middle East.
- **1988 onwards**: economic reforms.

steps.title: Problems
steps.body: Slower growth in later decades, political instability, over-dependence on remittances and foreign aid, volatile agricultural performance, rising external debt, and balance of payments crises requiring IMF support.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Identify the phase
steps.body: Government takes over steel and engineering firms → 1970s nationalisation. Opening sectors to private investors with Western loans → late 1970s/80s. Comprehensive reforms with IMF programmes → 1988 onwards.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Why growth faltered
steps.body: Growth often depended on good harvests and remittances rather than technological progress in industry → when these weakened, growth slowed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Pakistan followed a command economy like China.
- Ignoring the role of remittances.

activity.prompt: Order Pakistan’s phases

quiz.why: Pakistan's economy is mixed, with both public and private sectors. It is not purely command or barter, and 'feudal only' ignores its modern industry and services.

quiz.q: Nationalisation of capital goods industries in Pakistan was in the…
quiz.why: Pakistan nationalised its capital goods industries in the 1970s, then moved to denationalise later. The 1950s, 1990s and 2010s are not when this nationalisation took place.
Pakistan began its economic reforms in 1988. 1978 was China's start and 1991 was India's, which are the tempting wrong choices.

quiz.q: A key source of foreign exchange for Pakistan has been…
quiz.why: Money sent home by Pakistanis working abroad, called remittances, is a key source of foreign exchange for Pakistan. It is not mainly oil or software exports.

options: producing at home instead of importing
quiz.why: Import substitution means producing goods at home instead of importing them, usually protected by tariffs. It is the opposite of relying on imports or exports only.

scenes.text: Economists compare population, growth, sectors and human development.
China grew fastest and reduced poverty dramatically.
India’s growth rose after 1991, led by services.

steps.title: Demographic indicators
steps.body:
- **Population**: India is now the world’s most populous country (UN estimates, 2023); China’s population has begun to decline; Pakistan’s population is much smaller but growing faster.
- **Growth rate of population**: highest in Pakistan; lowest in China (one-child policy legacy).
- **Fertility rate**: low in China, higher in Pakistan.
- **Sex ratio**: below parity in all three; skewed in China partly due to son preference with one-child policy.
- **Urbanisation**: highest in China.

steps.title: GDP and sectors
steps.body: China has the largest GDP of the three and had very high growth (about 10% in many years of 1980–2010). In **China**, manufacturing (secondary sector) drove growth; in **India**, the **services** sector grew fastest; in **Pakistan**, growth slowed in the 1990s. Structural change: in China, the share of agriculture in employment fell sharply; in India, agriculture still employs the most workers.

steps.title: Human development indicators
steps.body: China ranks higher than India and Pakistan on the **Human Development Index** — higher life expectancy, lower infant and maternal mortality, higher literacy, lower poverty. India is ahead of Pakistan on many indicators. All three still have gaps in sanitation, health and education quality, and environmental pressures. **Liberty indicators** (democracy, freedoms) are also important in comparing development.

steps.title: Solved example 1: Read a comparison
steps.body: If China’s share of agriculture in GDP fell from ~30% to under 10% while India’s fell to ~16–18%, China’s structural change toward industry was faster.

steps.title: Solved example 2: Lessons
steps.body: China: early human-capital investment + market reforms + export manufacturing. India: democracy, services strength, need for manufacturing jobs and human development. Pakistan: need for stable policy, less reliance on remittances/aid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quoting precise current figures without sources — use trends.
- Ignoring freedom/liberty indicators when comparing development.

activity.prompt: Which country is described?

items.text: Growth led strongly by services after 1991
Highest population growth rate of the three

quiz.why: Among India, Pakistan and China, China has the highest Human Development Index, thanks to its better health, education and income indicators. The three are not equal.

quiz.q: India’s growth after 1991 was led by…
quiz.why: After 1991, India's growth was led by the services sector (IT, banking, telecom). Agriculture and manufacturing grew more slowly in share terms.

quiz.q: China’s growth was driven mainly by…
quiz.why: China's growth was driven mainly by manufacturing, helped by SEZs and exports. India's growth, in contrast, was mostly led by services.

quiz.q: Highest population growth rate among the three:
quiz.why: Pakistan has had the highest population growth rate among the three. China's growth rate is the lowest, helped by its one-child policy.
Liberty indicators measure freedoms such as democratic rights and freedom of expression. Exports, prices and GDP measure economic output, not freedom.

questions.q: India’s First Five Year Plan began in…
questions.why: India's First Five Year Plan began in 1951. China's was 1953 and Pakistan's was 1956; 1947 is when India became independent, which is tempting but wrong.

questions.q: China’s market reforms began in…
questions.why: China began its market reforms in 1978. 1958 was the Great Leap Forward, 1966 the Cultural Revolution and 1991 India's reforms.

questions.q: Pakistan’s reforms began in…
questions.why: Pakistan's reforms began in 1988. 1978 is China's year and 1991 is India's, so they are tempting but wrong.

questions.q: Great Leap Forward was launched in…
questions.why: The Great Leap Forward was launched in 1958 to speed up industrialisation. 1949 is the founding of the PRC and 1978 is the start of reforms.

questions.q: China follows (before 1978) a…
questions.why: Before 1978 China had a command (centrally planned) economy, where the state owned most resources and made the main decisions. A mixed economy was India's and Pakistan's choice.

questions.q: Dual pricing was introduced in…
questions.why: Dual pricing was a reform introduced in China, where output up to a quota sold at the state price and any extra at the market price. India, Pakistan and Nepal did not use this system.

questions.q: Assertion (A): China’s growth was led by manufacturing. Reason (R): China attracted FDI through SEZs and export industries.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true: China's growth was manufacturing-led, and attracting FDI through SEZs and export industries was how it built that manufacturing. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A country sends students to the countryside to learn from peasants (1966–76). Which?
questions.why: Sending students and officials to the countryside to learn from peasants (1966–76) was part of China's Cultural Revolution. India, Sri Lanka and Pakistan had no such campaign.

questions.q: Which has the highest HDI?
questions.why: China has the highest HDI of the three countries because of its better health, education and income measures. Pakistan has the lowest of the three.

questions.q: Case: A country nationalised capital goods industries in the 1970s and then denationalised. Which?
questions.why: Pakistan nationalised its capital goods industries in the 1970s and later denationalised them. That pattern does not describe India, China or Bangladesh.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The one-child policy contributed to an ageing population in China. Reason (R): Fewer births reduce the share of young people over time.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the one-child policy cut births, which meant fewer young people and a larger share of old people over time. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of China’s 1978 reforms?
questions.why: China's 1978 reforms allowed private firms, so abolishing all private enterprise is not a feature. The household responsibility system, dual pricing and SEZs were all part of them.

questions.q: Case: Growth in a country depends heavily on remittances and good harvests; it faced repeated BoP crises. Which?
questions.why: Pakistan's growth has depended on remittances and good harvests and it has had repeated balance of payments crises. China, India and Japan do not fit this description.

questions.q: Arrange first plans in order:
questions.why: In order of start: India 1951, China 1953, Pakistan 1956. The other orders mix up the dates.

questions.q: Case: Economists say a country did well on GDP but should also be judged on democratic freedoms. They are pointing to…
questions.why: Judging a country on democratic freedoms in addition to GDP refers to liberty indicators. Inflation, exports and sex ratio do not measure freedoms.

questions.q: India is now the world’s most populous country according to…
questions.why: According to UN estimates in 2023, India overtook China as the world's most populous country. The IMF and WTO do not publish this, and Census 2011 is older data.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Indian Economic Development
courses.summary: Fact sheet of dates, bodies and terms, model long answers, case-study practice and two mixed mock papers for Indian Economic Development.
outcomes: Learners can recall key dates and institutions without mix-ups
Learners can write balanced evaluative answers
Learners can apply concepts to news-style cases

lessons.title: Fact sheet: dates, bodies and terms

scenes.text: IED questions often test dates, names and terms.
A clean list helps you avoid mix-ups.
Here it is.

steps.title: Colonial and planning era
steps.body: Permanent Settlement 1793 · Railways 1850 · Suez Canal 1869 · First census 1881 · TISCO 1907 · Great divide 1921 · Life expectancy ~32 · IMR ~218 · Literacy <16% · Planning Commission 1950 · First Plan 1951 · Mahalanobis (2nd Plan) · IPR 1956 (3 categories) · Karve Committee 1955 · Green Revolution mid-1960s · NITI Aayog 1 Jan 2015.

steps.title: Reforms
steps.body: NEP July 1991 (LPG) · stabilisation vs structural · RBI regulator → facilitator · devaluation 1991 · QRs removed by 2001 · WTO 1995 (GATT 1948) · Navratna 1997 · demonetisation Nov 2016 · GST 1 July 2017.

steps.title: Human capital and rural
steps.body: RTE 2009 (6–14) · Kothari Commission 6% of GDP · NEP 2020 (5+3+3+4) · AICTE, UGC, NCERT, ICMR · NABARD 1982 · RRBs 1975 · SHGs/microcredit · MSP, FCI buffer stocks, PDS · Apni Mandi, Hadaspar, Rythu Bazar, Uzhavar Sandies · Operation Flood 1970.

steps.title: Employment, environment, neighbours
steps.body: WPR = workers/population × 100 · formal: 10+ workers · MGNREGA 2005 (100 days) · disguised/seasonal/open · CPCB 1974 · Montreal Protocol 1987 · Brundtland 1987 · Paris 2015 · China: PRC 1949, plan 1953, GLF 1958, Cultural Revolution 1966–76, reforms 1978, one-child 1979 · Pakistan: plan 1956, reforms 1988.

steps.title: Classic mix-ups
steps.body: GATT (1948) vs WTO (1995) · Planning Commission (1950) vs First Plan (1951) · global warming (CO₂) vs ozone depletion (CFCs) · China reforms 1978 vs India 1991 vs Pakistan 1988.

activity.prompt: Put these milestones in order

quiz.why: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of wage employment per year to each rural household that asks for unskilled manual work. 365 and 200 days are too high.
The World Trade Organization (WTO) replaced GATT in 1995. The IMF, World Bank and UNCTAD are separate institutions.
China began its reforms in 1978. 1958 was the Great Leap Forward, 1988 was Pakistan's start and 1991 was India's.
The Right to Education (RTE) Act covers free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14. Other age ranges are not the legal coverage.
NABARD, the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development, was set up in 1982. 1969 is the year of bank nationalisation, a tempting wrong choice.

scenes.text: IED long answers ask you to explain causes, evaluate policies or compare countries.
Examiners reward structure and balance.
Here are model outlines.

steps.title: Model answer 1: “Evaluate the Green Revolution.”
steps.body: Intro: HYV seeds + fertiliser + irrigation from mid-1960s. Positives: self-sufficiency, higher marketed surplus, buffer stocks, lower relative food prices. Negatives: regional and farmer inequality initially, overuse of chemicals and groundwater, dependence on subsidies. Conclusion: transformed food security; needs sustainable practices.

steps.title: Model answer 2: “Why did India need reforms in 1991?”
steps.body: Fiscal deficit and borrowing; BoP crisis with reserves for ~2 weeks of imports; inflation; Gulf war oil shock; IMF/World Bank loans → stabilisation + structural reforms (LPG).

steps.title: Model answer 3: “Compare China and India’s growth paths.”
steps.body: China: command economy till 1978, early human-capital and land reforms, then market reforms, SEZs, manufacturing-led growth. India: mixed economy, import substitution, 1991 reforms, services-led growth. Indicators: China higher HDI and faster structural change; India democratic, younger population. Lessons for both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- One-sided answers (only praise or only criticism).
- No conclusion.
- Inventing statistics — use trends if unsure.

activity.prompt: Write a 5-line answer: “Is MGNREGA a good policy?” Include one benefit, one criticism and a conclusion.
activity.hint: Benefits: rural income support, assets like ponds and roads, women’s participation. Criticisms: delays in wages, leakages, low-productivity work. Conclude with improvements.

quiz.why: A good evaluative answer weighs both sides, giving points for and against with reasons. One-sided, very short or date-only answers do not evaluate.
In 1991 India faced a balance of payments crisis: foreign exchange reserves had fallen so low they could pay for only a few weeks of imports. It was not a trade surplus or zero debt.
China's growth was led by manufacturing, while India's after 1991 was led by services. Agriculture and tourism were not the main drivers.
A common criticism of the Green Revolution is overuse of groundwater and chemicals. Self-sufficiency, higher output and buffer stocks are its benefits, not criticisms.

quiz.q: If unsure of a figure in an answer…
quiz.why: If you are unsure of a figure, describe the trend you know rather than invent a number. Accuracy matters more than adding a made-up value.

story.title: Reading economic news like an economist

scenes.text: Board papers include short cases from news.
Identify the concept, then explain with evidence.
Practise with these.

steps.title: Case 1
steps.body: “A state’s women’s SHGs saved ₹2 crore and got bank loans for dairy units.” → Concepts: SHGs, microcredit, diversification into animal husbandry, women’s empowerment.

steps.title: Case 2
steps.body: “Despite 7% GDP growth, formal jobs grew slowly and most new workers joined gig platforms.” → Concepts: jobless growth, informalisation; policy: skills, social security for gig workers.

steps.title: Case 3
steps.body: “A Punjab village shifted part of its paddy area to vegetables and adopted drip irrigation.” → Concepts: diversification, sustainable development (water conservation).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Naming a concept without quoting the line that proves it; ignoring the policy part of the question.

activity.prompt: Match the news line to the concept

quiz.why: Delivery riders working without Provident Fund or job security are in informal work, which shows informalisation of employment. Disinvestment and devaluation are different ideas.

quiz.q: “FCI procures wheat at MSP” relates to…
quiz.why: FCI buying wheat from farmers at the Minimum Support Price is part of agricultural marketing policy. It is not trade, monetary or tax policy.

quiz.q: “Wheat output rose sharply after HYV seeds in Punjab in the late 1960s” relates to…
quiz.why: Wheat output rising after HYV (high-yielding variety) seeds in Punjab in the late 1960s is the Green Revolution. Operation Flood is about milk and the Cultural Revolution is Chinese.

quiz.q: “Ozone layer recovering after CFC ban” relates to…
quiz.why: The ozone layer recovering after the CFC ban relates to the Montreal Protocol, which phased out CFCs. The Paris Agreement is about climate, and the WTO and GATT are about trade.

quiz.q: “Commune land divided into family plots” relates to…
quiz.why: Dividing commune land into family plots was part of China's 1978 reforms (the household responsibility system). It is not India's land ceiling, GST or Pakistan's nationalisation.

questions.q: [Mock A] Life expectancy in India around 1947:
questions.why: Life expectancy in India around independence was very low, about 32 years, due to poor health care and widespread disease. The higher figures describe later years.

questions.q: [Mock A] Architect of India’s Second Plan:
questions.why: P.C. Mahalanobis designed India's Second Five Year Plan, which stressed heavy industry. Deng Xiaoping led China's reforms and Verghese Kurien led Operation Flood.

questions.q: [Mock A] Tariff is a…
questions.why: A tariff is a tax on imports, which makes foreign goods dearer. A quota limits quantity, a licence is permission and a subsidy is a payment to producers.

questions.q: [Mock A] A farmer produces 150 quintals and keeps 50. Marketed surplus?
questions.why: Marketed surplus = output − what the farmer keeps = 150 − 50 = 100 quintals. It is the part sold in the market.

questions.q: [Mock A] Assertion (A): Colonial India had an export surplus. Reason (R): It was used to pay for British expenses in India.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true: colonial India had an export surplus, and it was used to meet British expenses in India. But the reason describes how the surplus was used, not why it arose, so it does not explain the assertion.

questions.q: [Mock A] Which is a structural reform of 1991?
questions.why: The 1991 structural reforms were long-term changes such as abolishing industrial licensing. Price controls, emergency loans and rationing are short-term measures.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: $1 = ₹60 becomes ₹75. A ₹1,500 Indian good costs a US buyer…
questions.why: At ₹60 per dollar, ₹1,500 costs 1,500 ÷ 60 = $25. At ₹75 per dollar it costs 1,500 ÷ 75 = $20, so the Indian good becomes cheaper for the US buyer.

questions.q: [Mock A] Human development treats education as…
questions.why: Human development treats education as an end in itself: it directly improves people's lives and freedoms, not merely as a tool for higher income.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: Population 3,000; workers 1,140. WPR?
questions.why: Worker Population Ratio = workers ÷ population × 100 = 1,140 ÷ 3,000 × 100 = 38%.

questions.q: [Mock A] Which channel is in Tamil Nadu?
questions.why: Uzhavar Sandies are farmers' markets in Tamil Nadu. Apni Mandi is Punjab/Haryana, Rythu Bazar is Andhra Pradesh and Hadaspar Mandi is Pune.

questions.q: [Mock A] Case: A state spends 3% of its ₹10 lakh crore GDP on education. Gap to 6% target?
questions.why: 3% of ₹10 lakh crore = ₹30,000 crore is spent now. 6% would be ₹60,000 crore, so the gap is ₹30,000 crore (the extra 3% of GDP).

questions.q: [Mock B] China’s Great Leap Forward year:
questions.why: The Great Leap Forward was launched in China in 1958. 1953 was China's First Plan, 1966 the Cultural Revolution and 1978 the market reforms.

questions.q: [Mock B] CPCB set up in:
questions.why: The Central Pollution Control Board was set up in 1974. 1987 and 2005 are other environmental or rural-employment dates, and 1950 is wrong.

questions.q: [Mock B] MGNREGA enacted in:
questions.why: MGNREGA was enacted in 2005 to guarantee rural wage employment. 1991 is the year of economic reforms and 2015 is the Paris Agreement.

questions.q: [Mock B] Disguised unemployment is common in…
questions.why: Disguised unemployment, where extra workers add nothing to output, is common in agriculture because many family members work on small farms. It is not typical of IT, banks or government offices.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: Labour force 2,500; unemployed 125. Unemployment rate?
questions.why: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100 = 125 ÷ 2,500 × 100 = 5%.

questions.q: [Mock B] Assertion (A): India’s growth after 1991 was services-led. Reason (R): Agriculture still employs the largest share of workers.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true: India's post-1991 growth was services-led, and agriculture still employs the largest share of workers. But the second does not explain why services led growth, so R does not explain A.

questions.q: [Mock B] Ozone depletion is mainly caused by…
questions.why: Ozone depletion is mainly caused by CFCs, which release chlorine in the stratosphere. CO₂ causes warming, and nitrogen and oxygen do not deplete ozone.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: A Chinese factory sells quota output at state price and extra output at market price. Policy?
questions.why: Selling quota output at the state price and the extra at the market price is dual pricing, a Chinese reform. MSP is India's price support and import substitution is a trade policy.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: 18 SHG members save ₹250 each per month for 2 years. Total savings?
questions.why: Total savings = members × monthly saving × months = 18 × 250 × 24 = ₹1,08,000. The other figures use the wrong number of months or members.

questions.q: [Mock B] Which statement is FALSE?
questions.why: India's First Five Year Plan began in 1951, not 1956, so that statement is false. The other three statements give correct dates.

questions.q: [Mock B] Case: GDP grows 9%, employment 1.8%. Employment elasticity?
questions.why: Employment elasticity = % change in employment ÷ % change in GDP = 1.8 ÷ 9 = 0.2.
